This describes every test in the corpus and why it is there. It is generated from
the cases themselves, so it cannot fall out of step with them.

## What this suite is for

Slice takes a variable font and gives you a smaller one. There are two programs
that do this: the original PyQt5 application by Source Foundry, and this
reimplementation. The suite exists to say, precisely and testably, what such a
program *should* do — and then to hold both of them to it.

The cases are data, not code. The same case runs against both programs, and a
single shared checker evaluates the result, so neither program marks its own
homework and no test can be quietly written in a way that flatters one of them.

Where the two disagree, the corpus is the arbiter, not either program. A case the
original fails is adjudicated on evidence: either the test is wrong and gets fixed,
or the original has a defect and this implementation must not copy it.

## The shape of a test

Each case names a fixture font, some editor input, and a list of things that must
be true of the result — or, for a bad input, the refusal that must come back. Each
also carries the behavioural claims it covers, from
[the behaviour map](original-behaviour.html), and a rationale saying why that is the
right answer.

Every case is labelled with where its authority comes from:

| label | meaning | cases |
|---|---|---|
| `spec` | the OpenType specification requires it | 86 |
| `fonttools` | inherited from fontTools, which the original delegates to | 106 |
| `slice-ui` | the application's own contract | 74 |
| `judgement` | a defensible design choice with no external authority | 34 |

There are **300 cases** in total, across 6 areas.
17 of them require removing overlaps, which the original never
had; it is expected to fail those, and that is not counted against it.

## axis-syntax

What happens to the text someone types into an axis cell. This is the tool's entire input language — a blank cell, a number, or a `min:max` range — so it is also where a mistyped entry either gets caught or turns into a font nobody asked for.

Covers claims: A2, B1, B10, B11, B12, B13, B2, B3, B4, B5, B6, B7, B8, B9, C1, C2, C3, C4, F1, F2, F3, G1, G2.

### `axis.blank-cell-leaves-axis-alone`

**An empty cell leaves that axis untouched and variable**

The editor's contract is that a cell is a request, so no text is no request: the axis must survive with the extent `fvar` already declared for it. Anything else would mean the user cannot pin one axis of a five-axis font without also restating the other four, and would make an untouched editor destructive. The four untouched axes are checked for their full original extents, not merely for their presence, because an implementation that silently narrowed an axis to its default location would otherwise pass.

<sub>covers B1, B2 · authority: `slice-ui` · fixture: `recursive-vf`</sub>

### `axis.mixed-pins-and-ranges`

**Pins, ranges and blank cells combine in one job**

Each cell is an independent request, so a job that pins one axis, restricts another and leaves three alone must apply all three readings in the same pass and preserve `fvar` order in what survives — the OpenType specification gives axis order meaning, since `gvar`, `avar` and the instance coordinate arrays are all indexed positionally against it. This is the shape of a realistic slice and the only case here that exercises the dispatch of B2 across several rows at once, which is where a parser that keeps state between rows would go wrong. The pinned axis must be gone, the restricted axis narrowed with its default intact, and the untouched axes unchanged.

<sub>covers B1, B2, B5, G2 · authority: `slice-ui` · fixture: `recursive-vf`</sub>

### `axis.pin-above-axis-maximum`

**A pin above the axis maximum is refused, not clamped**

This is B10, the weak suspect, and the argument turns on an asymmetry between pins and ranges. A range is an intersection: asking for `0:2000` on a 100-900 axis describes a design space that, intersected with what the font has, is exactly the whole axis, so clamping it gives the user what they asked for and B9 rightly leaves it alone. A pin is not an intersection but an assertion that a specific location exists; `wght=1200` on a 100-900 axis names a location the font does not define, there is no reading under which the user meant 900, and clamping produces a static font whose outlines and whose `usWeightClass` both silently differ from the request. Against that stands the real counter-argument, which is that clamping is fontTools' deliberate documented policy in `AxisTriple.limitRangeAndPopulateDefaults` and that a library caller relies on it — but that policy is written for a programmatic caller, whereas an editor cell is human input and validating human input before acting on it is the editor's job. My recommendation is therefore to refuse; if adjudication prefers the softer verdict, the honest encoding is success plus the proposed `warns` check, never silent success.

<sub>covers B10 · authority: `judgement` · fixture: `centred-default` · expects a refusal mentioning `wght`, `1200`, `axis`</sub>

### `axis.pin-at-axis-extremes`

**Pins exactly at an axis minimum and maximum are valid locations**

The `fvar` minValue and maxValue are inclusive bounds on the coordinates an axis may take, so the endpoints are locations the font defines and must be accepted. This case exists to fence the out-of-range rule encoded in `axis.pin-above-axis-maximum`: a bounds check written with the wrong comparison operator would reject the two most commonly requested locations in the whole design space, since "the heaviest weight" and "the full slant" are what most users of a variable font actually want to slice out.

<sub>covers B3, B10 · authority: `spec` · fixture: `recursive-vf`</sub>

### `axis.pin-below-axis-minimum`

**A pin below the axis minimum is refused, not clamped**

The same adjudication as `axis.pin-above-axis-maximum`, on the low side, which is a distinct branch in any bounds check and a distinct mistake in practice: `wght` on this fixture starts at 300, and 100 is what a user types who is thinking of the CSS weight scale or of a different family in the same superfamily. Clamping turns that misunderstanding into a font pinned at 300 with `usWeightClass` 300 and no indication that the request was altered. The original does not check bounds at all and is expected to fail this case.

<sub>covers B10 · authority: `judgement` · fixture: `recursive-vf` · expects a refusal mentioning `wght`, `100`, `axis`</sub>

### `axis.pin-decimal`

**A decimal pin lands at the fractional location, not at a rounded one**

OpenType stores axis coordinates as `Fixed` 16.16, which carries roughly four decimal digits of fraction, so 0.25 is exactly representable and there is no licence to round it to an integer. Fractional coordinates are ordinary in practice: registered axes such as `slnt` and Google Fonts registry axes such as `CRSV` are routinely used at intermediate positions, and `CRSV` here has a fractional default of 0.5 to begin with. Comparing outlines against the source drawn at CRSV 0.25 verifies the parsed value reached the instancer intact rather than merely that some pin happened.

<sub>covers B2, B3 · authority: `spec` · fixture: `recursive-vf`</sub>

### `axis.pin-decimal-comma-is-refused`

**A comma decimal separator is refused rather than truncated**

`400,5` is how a large part of the world writes four hundred and a half, and it is precisely the input a tool must not guess at: reading it as 400, as 4005, or as 400.5 are all defensible readings and all of them silently produce a font at a location the user did not verify. B4's contract — refuse the cell and name the axis — is the right answer because it puts the ambiguity back in front of the person who can resolve it. The original already refuses this, since `float()` does, and the case is here to keep a more permissive number parser from being introduced as a convenience.

<sub>covers B3, B4 · authority: `slice-ui` · fixture: `centred-default` · expects a refusal mentioning `wght`, `not a valid`</sub>

### `axis.pin-inf-is-refused`

**A pin of "inf" is refused**

`Fixed` 16.16 spans roughly -32768 to +32767.99998 and has no encoding for infinity, so an infinite coordinate cannot be written to `fvar`, to `gvar`, or to an `avar` segment map. Whatever a downstream conversion does with it — saturate, wrap, or raise — is an accident rather than the user's request. The original accepts this input for the same reason it accepts NaN, and is expected to fail this case; B11's proposed verdict is to reject non-finite values, and infinity is the other half of that set.

<sub>covers B3, B11 · authority: `spec` · fixture: `recursive-vf` · expects a refusal mentioning `wght`, `inf`</sub>

### `axis.pin-integer-with-trailing-zero`

**"400.0" and "400" name the same location**

The corpus deliberately treats `"400"` and `"400.0"` as different inputs because they are different characters; this case establishes that they are nonetheless the same request. Nothing in `Fixed` 16.16 distinguishes them, and the read-only column of the editor itself displays defaults with a trailing `.0`, so a user copying the displayed value back into the edit cell is typing the form under test here. An implementation whose numeric grammar required either the presence or the absence of a fractional part would fail one of these two spellings.

<sub>covers B3 · authority: `slice-ui` · fixture: `centred-default`</sub>

### `axis.pin-lone-minus-sign-is-refused`

**A lone minus sign is refused**

A half-typed value is the most likely thing to be sitting in a cell when a user reaches for the Slice button, and it denotes no location at all. The interesting risk is not that a tool accepts it as a number but that a lenient parser reads the sign and no digits as zero: on this fixture zero is inside the `slnt` range and is also its default, so the job would succeed and produce a font that looks entirely reasonable while ignoring what was typed. Refusing is the only reading that cannot silently be wrong.

<sub>covers B3, B4 · authority: `slice-ui` · fixture: `recursive-vf` · expects a refusal mentioning `slnt`, `not a valid`</sub>

### `axis.pin-nan-is-refused`

**A pin of "nan" is refused**

OpenType axis coordinates are `Fixed` 16.16 — a scaled integer format with no bit pattern reserved for NaN — so there is no such thing as an axis pinned to NaN and no way to write the request out. Worse, the value does not stop at the coordinate: normalizing NaN yields NaN, and every delta scaled by that normalized location becomes NaN, so a single mistyped cell can poison every outline in the font while the save still appears to succeed. The original accepts this input because its pin parser is bare `float()`, and it is expected to fail this case; that is the defect B11 records. The refusal must name the axis so the user can find the cell.

<sub>covers B3, B11 · authority: `spec` · fixture: `recursive-vf` · expects a refusal mentioning `CRSV`, `nan`</sub>

### `axis.pin-negative-decimal`

**A negative decimal pin is accepted and lands at the negative location**

The OpenType axis registry defines `slnt` as degrees of counter-clockwise rotation with negative values for the usual forward lean, so negative coordinates are not an edge case on this axis but the only useful half of it. `Fixed` 16.16 is signed, so -7.5 is exactly representable. A parser that mistook the leading minus for a separator, or that dropped the sign, would still produce a plausible-looking font, so the case is checked against the source outlines at slnt -7.5 rather than against the axis list alone.

<sub>covers B2, B3 · authority: `spec` · fixture: `recursive-vf`</sub>

### `axis.pin-negative-infinity-word-is-refused`

**A pin of "-Infinity" is refused, in any spelling or case**

`float()` accepts `inf`, `INF`, `Infinity` and `-Infinity` interchangeably, so an implementation that rejects only the literal three-letter lowercase spelling has closed one door of several into the same unrepresentable value. This case is not a duplicate of `axis.pin-inf-is-refused`: it pins down that the rejection is a property of the value, not a blocklisted string, and it exercises the negative side, which is the side a `slnt` user would reach for. `Fixed` 16.16 has no representation for either signed infinity.

<sub>covers B3, B11 · authority: `spec` · fixture: `recursive-vf` · expects a refusal mentioning `slnt`, `infinity`</sub>

### `axis.pin-non-numeric-word-is-refused`

**A style name typed into an axis cell is refused**

Axis cells take user-space coordinates, not style names: `fvar` has no mapping from the word "bold" to a location, and the mapping that does exist — the named-instance table — is not what this editor edits. Guessing would be actively harmful because a font's own named instances may place "Bold" anywhere on the axis. The message must contain the axis tag so that a user with five rows in front of them knows which cell to fix, which is the whole point of B4's wording.

<sub>covers B3, B4, F2 · authority: `slice-ui` · fixture: `recursive-vf` · expects a refusal mentioning `wght`, `not a valid`</sub>

### `axis.pin-plain-integer`

**A plain integer is a pin, and the pinned axis leaves the design space**

A cell with no colon names a single location, and an axis at a single location is no longer a variation axis: the OpenType specification requires an `fvar` axis record to describe a range of user-space values, so an axis fixed at one value has nothing left to declare and must be removed along with the variation data indexed by it. Pinning the only axis therefore yields a static font. `usWeightClass` is checked because `varLib.set_default_weight_width_slant` derives it from the pinned `wght` location, which makes it cheap evidence that the number the parser produced was 700 and not merely some number.

<sub>covers B2, B3, G1 · authority: `slice-ui` · fixture: `centred-default`</sub>

### `axis.pin-scientific-notation`

**Exponent notation is a finite number and is accepted**

B11's proposed verdict is narrow and deliberate: reject non-finite values, not reject everything `float()` happens to accept. `1e3` denotes 1000 unambiguously in every numeric grammar in common use, it is exactly representable in `Fixed` 16.16, and refusing it would buy nothing. The verified consequence is `usWeightClass` 1000, which distinguishes a correct parse from the failure mode this input actually invites, namely reading only the leading `1`. Note the deliberate asymmetry with `axis.range-scientific-notation-is-refused`: the pin grammar is `float()`, the range grammar is the B5 regular expression, and only the latter has no production for an exponent.

<sub>covers B3, B11 · authority: `judgement` · fixture: `recursive-vf`</sub>

### `axis.pin-surrounded-by-whitespace`

**A pin padded with spaces is accepted as the trimmed number**

Leading and trailing whitespace is an artefact of typing and of pasting values out of a specimen or a spreadsheet, never a statement about the design space, so it must be trimmed rather than treated as corruption. The original already behaves this way for pins because `float()` strips surrounding whitespace, and B11 records that as a property of the parser rather than as a defect. Fixing it here as required behaviour matters because the corrected B12 rule ("the whole cell must parse") is otherwise easy to implement as a regex anchored on the raw cell, which would reject this input and every pasted value like it.

<sub>covers B3, B11 · authority: `slice-ui` · fixture: `centred-default`</sub>

### `axis.pin-underscore-separator-is-refused`

**A Python-style digit separator is not a number**

`float("1_000")` returns 1000.0 because underscores are permitted in Python numeric literals, which is an implementation detail of the language the original was written in and not a numeric syntax any user of a font tool expects or any specification recognizes. Requiring every future implementation to reproduce it would be reproducing a leak rather than a behaviour, and refusing it costs a user nothing they cannot express as `1000`. The original is expected to fail this case; the divergence is small, deliberate, and of the same character as B11's.

<sub>covers B3, B4 · authority: `judgement` · fixture: `recursive-vf` · expects a refusal mentioning `wght`, `1_000`</sub>

### `axis.range-basic`

**A colon makes the cell a restricted range, and the axis survives narrowed**

The colon is the sole discriminator between the two things a cell can mean (B2), and a range must keep the axis in `fvar` with the requested bounds rather than pinning it. Named instances are checked to sit inside the new extent because the OpenType specification requires an `fvar` instance's coordinates to lie within each axis's declared range, so any instance the narrowing left outside would make the output non-conformant. The default is required to stay at 400: a Level 3 restriction moves the bounds and nothing else.

<sub>covers B2, B5, G2 · authority: `slice-ui` · fixture: `centred-default`</sub>

### `axis.range-cell-padded-with-whitespace`

**A range padded with leading and trailing whitespace is accepted**

This case exists to say precisely what B12's corrected rule means, because the obvious implementation of it gets this wrong. The B5 expression begins at `start` with no leading `\s*`, so switching `re.search` for `re.fullmatch` on the raw cell would reject a leading space while still accepting a trailing one — an arbitrary distinction the user cannot see. The rule is therefore: trim the cell, then require the remainder to parse in its entirety. That also keeps the range path consistent with the pin path, which tolerates surrounding whitespace (B11) and must continue to.

<sub>covers B5, B12 · authority: `slice-ui` · fixture: `centred-default`</sub>

### `axis.range-collapsed-to-a-point`

**A range whose bounds are equal is a pin**

A range with minimum equal to maximum admits exactly one coordinate, and an `fvar` axis that admits one coordinate is not an axis: `fontTools` recognizes this explicitly, treating a triple whose bounds coincide as a pinned location and dropping the axis from `fvar`. Writing the axis out with min = default = max would be legal but pointless and would leave `gvar` deltas for a variation that can never vary. The `slnt` default of 0 is used so that the collapsed point is a location the axis genuinely contains, keeping this case about the collapse and not about bounds.

<sub>covers B5, B6, G2 · authority: `fonttools` · fixture: `recursive-vf`</sub>

### `axis.range-embedded-in-garbage-is-refused`

**A range buried in surrounding text is refused, not extracted**

This is B12. `re.search` finds the grammar anywhere in the cell, so `xyz200:700zzz` is accepted and the tool acts on a substring the user did not intend as their whole request. That is inconsistent with B4, under which any other cell the parser cannot make sense of is refused outright, and it hides exactly the typos a validator exists to catch. The corrected rule is that the trimmed cell must parse in its entirety; the original is expected to fail this case by succeeding.

<sub>covers B12 · authority: `slice-ui` · fixture: `centred-default` · expects a refusal mentioning `wght`, `not a valid`</sub>

### `axis.range-equal-to-full-extent`

**A range identical to the axis's own extent is accepted, not refused as a no-op**

The B13 refusal is worded as though it detected an unchanged design space, but what it actually tests is that at least one cell is non-empty, and that weaker test is the right one to keep. Deciding whether a request truly narrows anything would mean comparing the requested space against the font's after clamping, which would refuse `300:1000` here while accepting the equivalent `200:1000`, an inconsistency the user cannot predict. There is also legitimate work in a no-op slice, since the instancer still runs its optimizations. The obligation is only that the output remains a valid variable font with its design space intact.

<sub>covers B5, B13, F3 · authority: `judgement` · fixture: `recursive-vf`</sub>

### `axis.range-excluding-default-is-refused`

**A range that does not contain the axis default is refused**

An `fvar` axis record must satisfy minValue <= defaultValue <= maxValue, so a range of 400:700 on an axis whose default is 300 cannot be written without also moving the default — a different and larger operation (Level 4 sub-spacing) that changes what the font renders when no variation settings are applied, and that requires renormalizing every delta and every `avar` segment about the new origin. Honouring the range while leaving the default outside it would produce a malformed font; honouring it by moving the default would silently change the font's identity. Refusing, and naming both the range and the default in the message, is the correct answer for a tool that does not implement Level 4.

<sub>covers B7 · authority: `spec` · fixture: `recursive-vf` · expects a refusal mentioning `wght`, `default`</sub>

### `axis.range-excluding-negative-default-is-refused`

**The default-containment rule holds when the default is the upper bound**

Asking for -15:-5 on `slnt` excludes the default of 0, and this is the shape of the request a user most plausibly makes by mistake — "give me only the slanted part of the font" — precisely because the upright default feels like something they are discarding rather than something the format requires them to keep. A containment check written as `min <= default <= max` handles it, but one written for axes whose default is interior, or one comparing absolute values, does not. The refusal is required for the same reason as the previous case: the output would otherwise have defaultValue outside [minValue, maxValue].

<sub>covers B7 · authority: `spec` · fixture: `recursive-vf` · expects a refusal mentioning `slnt`, `default`</sub>

### `axis.range-exponent-bound-reads-as-its-value`

**An exponent in a range bound is read as its value, never truncated to the mantissa**

This is the most damaging instance of B12 the fixture admits. `300:1e3` means 300 to 1000 to anyone who writes it, but `re.search` matches `300:1`, sorts it to 1:300, finds the default of 300 inside, and accepts it; clamping then collapses the axis to 300:300 and the weight axis disappears from the font entirely. The user asked to keep the whole weight range and received a static weight, with no message. The corpus requires the bound to be read as 1000: fontTools' `parseLimits` reads `wght=300:1e3` as (300, 1000), and it is fontTools' instancer that Slice hands the result to, so a limit string a user learned from `fonttools varLib.instancer --help` must not mean something different here. The check is that the weight axis survives with its full extent; had `1e3` been read as 1 the axis would have been pinned away, which is exactly the failure being guarded against.

<sub>covers B12 · authority: `judgement` · fixture: `recursive-vf`</sub>

### `axis.range-exponent-bounds-on-both-sides`

**Exponents on both bounds give the range they spell, not the mantissas**

The companion to the `300:1e3` case, with a range that does not coincide with the axis extent, so the bounds themselves are observable rather than only the axis's survival. `3e2:7e2` must yield a weight axis running 300 to 700. The original reads it as neither: `re.search` scans forward until the pattern matches anywhere, finds `2:7` inside `3e2:7e2`, and refuses the cell because 2 to 7 does not contain the default of 300. Measured, not inferred -- it reports "The wght range 2.0:7.0 does not include the default axis value (300.0)". Success with the right extent therefore separates the correct reading from both the truncating one and the scanning one.

<sub>covers B12 · authority: `judgement` · fixture: `recursive-vf`</sub>

### `axis.range-leading-dot-bound-reads-as-a-fraction`

**A bound written with a leading decimal point is read as a fraction, never as its digits**

The original's range regex requires a digit before the decimal point, so `.25` is not a bound it can produce -- but `re.search` skips the dot and matches `25:1`, sorts it to 1:25, finds that the CRSV default of 0.5 is not inside, and refuses with "The CRSV range 1.0:25.0 does not include the default axis value (0.5)" -- naming back to the user a range they never typed. On a bound the regex happens to accept it does worse and reads the digits alone. Either way the user's `.25` is not what gets used. The corpus requires the bound to be read as a quarter, because that is what it means everywhere else: fontTools' own `parseLimits` -- the parser for the instancer Slice drives -- reads `wght=.5:900` as (0.5, 900), and so do strtod, Python's `float()` and JSON. Slice's pin parser already reads `.25` as a quarter, so refusing it one character later in the same cell would be an inconsistency the user cannot predict. Misreading it as 25 is the defect; reading it correctly, or refusing it outright, are the two defensible answers, and agreement with the reference implementation decides between them.

<sub>covers B12 · authority: `judgement` · fixture: `recursive-vf`</sub>

### `axis.range-missing-lower-bound-is-refused`

**A range with nothing before the colon is refused**

The mirror of the previous case, and a distinct code path: with `re.search` the missing bound is a failure to match at all, whereas a hand-written splitter is likely to produce an empty first field and hand it to a number parser. Either way the answer is the same, because `:400` names no lower bound and the tool must not guess one. Keeping both halves of the grammar fixed by cases is what stops an implementation from anchoring only one end.

<sub>covers B5, B4 · authority: `slice-ui` · fixture: `centred-default` · expects a refusal mentioning `wght`, `not a valid`</sub>

### `axis.range-missing-upper-bound-is-refused`

**A range with nothing after the colon is refused**

The B5 grammar requires a number on both sides of the colon, and there is no defensible completion of `400:` — reading the missing bound as the axis maximum would be inventing half the request, and reading it as equal to the start would silently turn a range into a pin. This is the state a cell is in mid-typing, so the tool must be able to say what is wrong with it rather than acting on it. The message names the axis, matching B4's contract for every other unparseable cell.

<sub>covers B5, B4 · authority: `slice-ui` · fixture: `centred-default` · expects a refusal mentioning `wght`, `not a valid`</sub>

### `axis.range-negative-bounds-reversed`

**A negative range typed in reverse order is sorted correctly**

Sorting has to be numeric, not lexicographic and not "first number is the minimum": on a negative axis the user's natural reading order is often from the default towards the extreme, so `0:-10` is how someone describes discarding the steep end. A comparison done on the parsed strings, or a sort that mishandles the sign, would produce minValue 0 and maxValue -10 and an `fvar` record the OpenType specification forbids. The expected extent is identical to `axis.range-with-default-at-maximum`, which is the point.

<sub>covers B5, B6 · authority: `slice-ui` · fixture: `recursive-vf`</sub>

### `axis.range-non-numeric-bounds-are-refused`

**Words either side of a colon are refused**

`min:max` is what a user types who has read the column header `Min : Max [Default]` as a template to fill in rather than as a description, so it is a realistic entry and not a contrived one. It also exercises B2's dispatch: the cell contains a colon, so it must be judged by the range grammar and refused there, rather than falling through to the pin parser and producing a message about a single numeric value that would not help. The refusal must name the axis.

<sub>covers B2, B5, B4 · authority: `slice-ui` · fixture: `centred-default` · expects a refusal mentioning `wght`, `not a valid`</sub>

### `axis.range-overshooting-extent-is-clamped`

**A range that overshoots one end of the axis is clamped to it**

A restriction is an intersection with what the font already has, so asking for 200:700 on an axis that starts at 300 describes exactly the design space 300:700 — the user has lost nothing and been told nothing untrue. This is `fontTools`' documented behaviour in `AxisTriple.limitRangeAndPopulateDefaults`, and unlike the pin case (B10) there is no divergence between the request and the result to warn about. Note the deliberate contrast with `axis.pin-below-axis-minimum`, which refuses the same number on the same axis: the corpus treats out-of-extent bounds as benign for ranges and as an error for pins, and the rationale there sets out why.

<sub>covers B9 · authority: `fonttools` · fixture: `recursive-vf`</sub>

### `axis.range-reversed-is-sorted`

**A range typed high-to-low means the same as low-to-high**

A range denotes a set of coordinates, and the `fvar` axis record has one slot for the smaller bound and one for the larger, so the order in which the user typed the two numbers carries no information that the format can store. Sorting is the only reading that does not throw input away; the alternatives are refusing a request whose meaning is unambiguous, or writing minValue greater than maxValue, which is malformed. The resulting extent is required to be identical to `axis.range-basic`, which is the whole content of the claim.

<sub>covers B5, B6 · authority: `slice-ui` · fixture: `centred-default`</sub>

### `axis.range-spaces-around-colon`

**Spaces around the colon are permitted**

The B5 grammar writes the separator as `\s*:\s*` deliberately, and the editor's own read-only column displays extents in exactly this spaced form (`100.0 : 900.0 [400.0]`), so a user who copies what the tool showed them and edits a number is typing this input. Refusing it would mean the tool cannot read back its own display. The check is that the spacing changes nothing about the resulting extent.

<sub>covers B5 · authority: `slice-ui` · fixture: `centred-default`</sub>

### `axis.range-wholly-outside-extent-is-refused`

**A range entirely outside the axis is judged as typed, not as clamped**

1000:2000 on a 100-900 axis is out of range and also excludes the default, and the order of the two checks decides the outcome: validate the literal request and it is refused for excluding the default of 400, but clamp first and it collapses to 900:900, which contains no default either but looks to a naive check like a pin. The user's request must be judged as typed, because the message they receive has to describe the cell they can see. This also fixes the boundary of B9's leniency: clamping is a courtesy applied to ranges that genuinely overlap the axis, not a licence to reinterpret a request that has nothing in common with it.

<sub>covers B7, B9 · authority: `spec` · fixture: `centred-default` · expects a refusal mentioning `wght`, `default`</sub>

### `axis.range-with-default-at-maximum`

**A range is valid when the default sits on its upper bound**

Recursive's `slnt` runs -15 to 0 with the default at 0, so its default is the upper bound and its useful values are all negative — the mirror image of the previous case and a second inclusive boundary that an off-by-one validator would get wrong. Restricting it to -10:0 keeps the upright default and discards the steepest third of the slant, which is a real editorial request. Together with `axis.range-with-default-at-minimum` this fixes both ends of the inclusive containment rule.

<sub>covers B5, B7 · authority: `spec` · fixture: `recursive-vf`</sub>

### `axis.range-with-default-at-minimum`

**A range is valid when the default sits on its lower bound**

Recursive's `wght` has its default equal to its minimum, which is a common shape for an axis whose regular weight is its lightest (and the shape the `single-axis-min-default` fixture exists to isolate). The Level 3 requirement is that the restricted range contain the default, and containment is inclusive: the OpenType specification requires only that minValue <= defaultValue <= maxValue. A validator written with a strict comparison would reject every narrowing of an axis of this shape, which is most of what a user would want to do with this font.

<sub>covers B5, B7 · authority: `spec` · fixture: `recursive-vf`</sub>

### `axis.range-with-new-default-is-refused`

**A trailing [default] group asking to move the default is refused, not discarded**

This is B8. The original parses `[700]`, understands it as a request to relocate the default, and then throws it away, returning a font whose default is still 300 with nothing said — so the program demonstrably knows what was asked and declines to admit it cannot do it. The user's request is not met and their font is not what they asked for. Moving the default is Level 4 sub-spacing, which `fontTools`' instancer has since gained support for through its `min:default:max` triple limits, so an implementation may legitimately implement it; what it may not do is accept the syntax and ignore the meaning. The original is expected to fail this case, and the message must name both the axis and the default so the user knows which part of the cell was refused.

<sub>covers B8 · authority: `slice-ui` · fixture: `recursive-vf` · expects a refusal mentioning `wght`, `default`</sub>

### `axis.range-with-three-parts-is-refused`

**A cell with two colons is refused rather than truncated to the first range**

`200:700:900` is not noise but a coherent request in another notation: it is exactly `fontTools`' own `min:default:max` triple syntax for Level 4 sub-spacing, so a user coming from `fonttools varLib.instancer` will type it. Under `re.search` the original quietly keeps `200:700` and discards the rest, delivering a font with a different default from the one requested — the same silent reinterpretation as B8, reached by a different route. Refusing is required until the syntax is actually supported; the original is expected to fail this case.

<sub>covers B12 · authority: `slice-ui` · fixture: `centred-default` · expects a refusal mentioning `wght`, `not a valid`</sub>

### `axis.range-with-trailing-words-is-refused`

**A range followed by stray text is refused**

`400:700 garbage` is the shape B12 takes in practice — a note, a unit, or a fragment of a previous edit left after the numbers — and `re.search` accepts it silently. The trailing text may well be the user's own annotation contradicting the numbers, and the tool has no way to know. Requiring the whole trimmed cell to parse refuses it and asks; this is the same rule as `axis.range-embedded-in-garbage-is-refused` applied where the noise follows rather than surrounds, which is the case a fix anchored only at the start of the string would still get wrong. The original is expected to fail this case.

<sub>covers B12 · authority: `slice-ui` · fixture: `centred-default` · expects a refusal mentioning `wght`, `not a valid`</sub>

### `axis.range-with-unchanged-default-is-honoured`

**A [default] group naming the default the axis already has is satisfiable, and is honoured**

B8's defect is accepting a request the tool cannot satisfy; it is not the bracket syntax itself. Here the user restricts wght to 200:700 and states that the default is 400, which is what `fvar` already says, so the resulting font matches the request exactly and there is nothing left unhonoured. Refusing would be pedantry with a cost, since a user documenting the full intended triple in one cell — the natural thing to do after reading the `Min : Max [Default]` column header — would be turned away for asking for what they were already getting. An implementation that refuses every bracket group unconditionally will fail this case; that is the adjudication this case is here to force, and the deciding question is whether the output can satisfy the request as written.

<sub>covers B8, B5 · authority: `judgement` · fixture: `centred-default`</sub>

### `editor.axis-names-prefer-the-registries`

**Each row is labelled with the registered or registry name for its tag**

A four-character tag is not self-explanatory to most users, and the two authorities that give it a name are the OpenType design-variation axis tag registry, which fixes "Weight" for `wght` and "Slant" for `slnt`, and the Google Fonts axis registry, which fixes "Monospace", "Casual" and "Cursive" for `MONO`, `CASL` and `CRSV`. Preferring those over the font's own `name` entry (C4) means the label is stable across every font that uses the tag, so a user reads the same word for the same axis regardless of who compiled the font — which is the entire value of a registered tag. The font's own axis name remains the fallback for tags in neither registry. Note that this fixture cannot fully separate the two sources, since Recursive's own axis names agree with the registries; a fixture whose `name` table disagrees would be needed to prove the precedence rather than the outcome.

<sub>covers C3, C4 · authority: `slice-ui` · fixture: `recursive-vf`</sub>

### `editor.rows-follow-fvar-order-and-show-extents`

**The editor shows one row per fvar axis, in order, with that axis's extent**

Axis order in `fvar` is meaningful — `gvar` tuple coordinates, `avar` segment maps and instance coordinate arrays are all indexed positionally against it — so displaying the rows in that order is what lets a user check the editor against any other tool's view of the same font. The read-only column exists to state, per axis, what the font actually permits, so it must carry the `fvar` minimum, maximum and default and no derived or rounded substitute; it is the only thing telling the user which values their cell may contain. Five rows are required for this five-axis font, which also fixes that the editor's fixed five-row scaffold is replaced on load rather than padded out.

<sub>covers C1, C2 · authority: `slice-ui` · fixture: `recursive-vf`</sub>

### `editor.single-axis-font-shows-one-row`

**A one-axis font shows exactly one row**

The original's model is built around a five-row scaffold that is replaced when a font loads, so the number of rows shown must come from `fvar` and not from that scaffold: a one-axis font that displayed four empty rows would invite entries against axes the font does not have. This fixture's off-centre default of 400 within 100-900 also pins down that the third number in the read-only column is the default and not, say, the midpoint of the extent, which a two-axis font with a centred default could not distinguish.

<sub>covers C1, C2 · authority: `slice-ui` · fixture: `centred-default`</sub>

### `editor.static-font-is-refused-on-load`

**A font with no fvar is refused at load, not silently accepted as a font with no axes**

`fvar` is what makes a font variable, and a font without one has no design space to build a sub-space from -- there is nothing the tool could do to it but copy it. The failure mode being guarded against is not a crash but a plausible-looking success: an implementation that treats a missing `fvar` as 'a font with zero axes' presents an empty Axis Editor and then writes out a copy, and the user has no way to tell that from a slice that happened to change nothing. Both programs refuse, and the message must name `fvar` so the reason is discoverable rather than merely stated.

<sub>covers A2 · authority: `slice-ui` · fixture: `static-ttf` · expects a refusal mentioning `fvar`</sub>

### `slice.all-cells-blank-is-refused`

**With every cell blank the job is refused**

Every blank cell means "leave this axis alone" (B1), so all cells blank means the user has described the font they already have. Producing a copy would be a silent no-op that a user could easily mistake for a successful slice, and the tool has enough information to say so before opening a save dialog. The refusal must explain what to do next rather than merely reporting failure, which is why the message is required to say that at least one axis must be given a location or a range.

<sub>covers B13, F3, B1 · authority: `slice-ui` · fixture: `recursive-vf` · expects a refusal mentioning `at least one`, `axis`</sub>

### `slice.first-invalid-cell-is-reported`

**With several bad cells the message names at least the first one in fvar order**

When two cells are unparseable the user needs a message that corresponds to something on screen, and the rows are displayed in `fvar` order (C1), so the first offender in that order is the one they will look at first. Requiring the message to contain `wght` — the earlier of the two bad rows here — is satisfied both by a tool that reports the first error and by one that reports all of them, and excludes only a tool that picks an arbitrary row, which is the behaviour that leaves a user staring at a cell that looks fine. This is `judgement`: nothing external settles the reporting order, but it must be predictable.

<sub>covers F2, B4, C1 · authority: `judgement` · fixture: `recursive-vf` · expects a refusal mentioning `wght`</sub>

### `slice.invalid-cell-aborts-before-any-output`

**One bad cell abandons the whole job, including the valid cells**

Validation covers the whole form before any work starts, so a valid `MONO` pin alongside an unparseable `CRSV` cell must produce no font at all rather than a font sliced on the cells that happened to parse. Partial application would be the worst outcome available: the user receives a file that looks like a successful slice but silently omits one of their requests. The corpus's definition of an `error` outcome already forbids a written-out font, which is exactly the property under test here; the message must name `CRSV` so the user knows which of the five rows to fix.

<sub>covers F2, B4 · authority: `slice-ui` · fixture: `recursive-vf` · expects a refusal mentioning `CRSV`, `not a valid`</sub>

### `slice.no-font-loaded-is-refused`

**Slicing with no font loaded refuses and does nothing**

There is nothing to slice and, more to the point, nothing to validate the axis values against: the axis rows, their extents and their defaults all come from `fvar`, so with no font loaded even a well-formed `400` cannot be checked or applied. The tool must say what is missing and stop, and must not write a file or raise an unhandled error. The message is required to mention the font so it identifies what to do next.

<sub>covers F1 · authority: `slice-ui` · fixture: `recursive-vf` · expects a refusal mentioning `font`</sub>

### `slice.only-whitespace-cells-is-refused-as-blank`

**Cells holding only whitespace still count as an empty request**

The consequence of the previous case at the level of the whole job: if whitespace trims to blank, then a form containing nothing but whitespace is a blank form and must be refused with B13's message, telling the user to define an axis. The distinction matters because both implementations refuse this input and only the message separates them — the original quotes the whitespace back as an invalid axis value, which describes a problem the user cannot see, while the required message describes what is actually missing.

<sub>covers B13, F3 · authority: `judgement` · fixture: `recursive-vf` · expects a refusal mentioning `at least one`, `axis`</sub>

### `slice.whitespace-only-cell-counts-as-blank`

**A cell holding only spaces is treated as untouched**

A cell containing two spaces is indistinguishable on screen from an empty one, so the two must mean the same thing; a user cannot debug a message about a value they cannot see. This follows directly from the trim-then-parse rule that `axis.pin-surrounded-by-whitespace` and `axis.range-cell-padded-with-whitespace` establish — trimming this cell leaves the empty string, which is B1's "leave the axis alone". The original instead reaches `float("  ")` and refuses the job with a message quoting whitespace, so it is expected to fail this case; the divergence is small and deliberate, and the alternative reading (refuse, because stray input is worth reporting) is defensible but loses on the fact that the user cannot see what they are being told about.

<sub>covers B1, B13 · authority: `judgement` · fixture: `recursive-vf`</sub>

## bitflags

`OS/2.fsSelection` and `head.macStyle`: the bits that tell software whether a font is regular, bold or italic. Six of them are editable; the rest must survive untouched.

Covers claims: A5, E1, E2, E3, E4, E5, G1, G2, G7, H1.

### `bitflags.all-six-cleared-preserves-unexposed`

**Clearing all six checkboxes clears only those six**

This is the worst case for bit preservation: every checkbox the editor owns is explicitly unticked, so a correct implementation must clear precisely bits 0, 5, 6 and 8 of fsSelection and bits 0 and 1 of macStyle, and nothing else. The fixture's 0xC0 must become 0x80 = 128, keeping bit 7 USE_TYPO_METRICS, and macStyle must stay 0. If an implementation ever writes 0 to fsSelection here it has thrown away the OS/2 specification's vertical-metrics opt-in along with the style bits.

<sub>covers E1, E2, E3 · authority: `spec` · fixture: `recursive-vf`</sub>

### `bitflags.all-six-set-preserves-unexposed`

**Setting all six checkboxes ORs in only those six**

Setting every exposed bit must be a pure OR against the font's existing value: 0xC0 with bits 0, 5, 6 and 8 added is 0x1E1 = 481, and macStyle 0 with bits 0 and 1 added is 3. Bit 7 USE_TYPO_METRICS must survive, and no bit the editor does not name may appear. The result is maximally self-contradictory -- the OS/2 specification makes bit 6 REGULAR mutually exclusive with bits 0 ITALIC and 5 BOLD -- and the corpus position is that this is written as asked and reported as a warning, not refused; see bitflags.contradiction-not-refused.

<sub>covers E1, E2, E3, E5 · authority: `spec` · fixture: `recursive-vf`</sub>

### `bitflags.bits-survive-full-instancing`

**Bits set by the user survive a full static instantiation**

Instancing rewrites OS/2 (usWeightClass, usWidthClass, xAvgCharWidth) and head, so the order of operations matters: the original edits the bits after instantiateVariableFont returns, and any implementation must do the same or apply the edit to the final tables. With every axis pinned the output is a static font, and the requested fsSelection 0xA0 = 160 and macStyle 1 must be what is on disk. If the bits were applied before instancing and fontTools rewrote the field, this case would catch it.

<sub>covers E3, G1 · authority: `slice-ui` · fixture: `recursive-vf`</sub>

### `bitflags.bits-survive-partial-instancing`

**Bits set by the user survive a restricted-range slice**

A partial instance keeps fvar and takes a different code path through fontTools than a full pin, but OS/2 and head are edited the same way afterwards, so the user's bits must come out identical. Restricting wght to 300:700 keeps all five axes and must leave fsSelection at 0x1C0 = 448 -- the fixture's bits 6 and 7 plus the requested bit 8 WWS. Asserting the axis count alongside the bits shows the two edits are independent.

<sub>covers E3, G2 · authority: `slice-ui` · fixture: `recursive-vf`</sub>

### `bitflags.bold-bit-does-not-change-usweightclass`

**Setting BOLD does not move OS/2.usWeightClass**

OS/2.usWeightClass is a numeric weight on the 1-1000 scale and fsSelection bit 5 BOLD is a style-map flag; the OS/2 specification defines them separately and nothing in it licenses deriving one from the other. fontTools sets usWeightClass from the pinned wght location, so pinning wght at 400 must give 400 even though the user has declared the instance Bold. Conflating them would silently overwrite a value the slicing operation computed from the design space with a guess derived from a checkbox.

<sub>covers E3, G7 · authority: `spec` · fixture: `recursive-vf`</sub>

### `bitflags.bold-bit-on-light-weight-is-allowed`

**BOLD may be declared on a light instance without altering usWeightClass**

Pinning wght at the fixture's default of 300 gives usWeightClass 300, and the user may still want that instance to be the Bold member of a two-style family -- a legitimate arrangement for a light display family, and one the OS/2 specification does not forbid, since it nowhere ties bit 5 to a usWeightClass threshold. The tool must therefore write fsSelection 0xA0 = 160 and macStyle 1 while leaving usWeightClass at 300, and must not treat the pairing as an error. This is a bound on how far consistency checking may go: it covers the relationships the specifications actually state, not plausible-looking ones.

<sub>covers E3, E5, G7 · authority: `judgement` · fixture: `recursive-vf`</sub>

### `bitflags.consistent-bold-italic-pair`

**A coherent Bold Italic declaration sets all four style bits**

Bold Italic is the fourth RIBBI style and the only one that legitimately sets two bits in each field: fsSelection bits 0 and 5, bit 6 clear, and macStyle bits 0 and 1. That is 0xA1 = 161 and 3, with bit 7 USE_TYPO_METRICS preserved. It is worth a case of its own because 0xA1 and the contradictory 0xE1 of bitflags.contradiction-not-refused differ by one bit, and an implementation that confuses mutual exclusion with a blanket ban on multiple bits would reject or mangle this conformant combination.

<sub>covers E1, E2, E3, E5 · authority: `spec` · fixture: `recursive-vf`</sub>

### `bitflags.consistent-bold-pair`

**A coherent Bold declaration sets both fields and clears REGULAR**

This is what a correct Bold declaration looks like under both specifications at once: fsSelection bit 5 BOLD set, bit 6 REGULAR cleared because the OS/2 specification makes it mutually exclusive with bit 5, and head.macStyle bit 0 Bold set because the head specification requires the two to agree. The result must be fsSelection 0xA0 = 160, retaining bit 7 USE_TYPO_METRICS, and macStyle 1. The case matters as the negative control for E5: a conformant combination must not draw a warning, or the warning carries no information.

<sub>covers E1, E2, E3, E5 · authority: `spec` · fixture: `recursive-vf`</sub>

### `bitflags.consistent-italic-pair`

**A coherent Italic declaration sets both fields and clears REGULAR**

Pinning slnt at -15 produces an oblique instance, and fontTools sets post.italicAngle from the pinned location but never the style bits, so declaring the instance italic is the user's job. The conformant declaration is fsSelection bit 0 ITALIC set with bit 6 REGULAR cleared (mutual exclusion, OS/2) and head.macStyle bit 1 Italic set (agreement, head), giving 0x81 = 129 and 2. Like the Bold pair, this is a negative control for the E5 warning.

<sub>covers E1, E2, E3, E5 · authority: `spec` · fixture: `recursive-vf`</sub>

### `bitflags.contradiction-fsselection-bold-without-macstyle-bold`

**fsSelection BOLD without macStyle BOLD is written as asked**

The head specification requires macStyle bits 0 Bold and 1 Italic to be consistent with OS/2.fsSelection bits 5 BOLD and 0 ITALIC; the two fields are duplicate declarations read by different platforms, and disagreement means an application picks a different style depending on which field it trusts. Ticking fsSelection bit 5 while leaving macStyle bit 0 unticked produces exactly that split -- fsSelection 0xA0 = 160 with macStyle 0 -- and the corpus requires it to be written, with a warning, rather than auto-mirrored. Auto-mirroring would be a second silent rewrite of the user's request, of the same species as the E4 defect.

<sub>covers E5 · authority: `judgement` · fixture: `recursive-vf`</sub>

### `bitflags.contradiction-macstyle-italic-without-fsselection`

**macStyle ITALIC without fsSelection ITALIC is written as asked**

This is the mirror of the previous case, in the direction the head specification names: macStyle bit 1 Italic set while OS/2.fsSelection bit 0 ITALIC stays clear. The two fields must agree, so the output (macStyle 2, fsSelection 192 with bit 0 clear) is non-conformant and the user should be told. It is still written, because the editor's contract is that a ticked box means that bit, and because a font being repaired may legitimately pass through this state between edits.

<sub>covers E5 · authority: `judgement` · fixture: `recursive-vf`</sub>

### `bitflags.contradiction-not-refused`

**A wholly contradictory bit combination is a warning, never a refusal**

Setting ITALIC, BOLD and REGULAR at once violates the OS/2 specification's mutual exclusion twice over, and is the strongest case anyone could make for refusing the job. The corpus deliberately requires success, with fsSelection 0xE1 = 225 and macStyle 3, because refusing would make the tool unable to produce a font it can read: OS/2 permits these bits to be written and real fonts in the wild already carry contradictory combinations, so a hard error would block the very repair the operator came to make. The distinguishing check -- that the tool said something -- is the proposed warns check; without it this case only establishes that the job is not refused.

<sub>covers E5 · authority: `judgement` · fixture: `recursive-vf`</sub>

### `bitflags.contradiction-regular-and-bold`

**REGULAR together with BOLD is written as asked**

The OS/2 specification states that fsSelection bit 6 REGULAR is mutually exclusive with bits 0 ITALIC and 5 BOLD -- if bit 6 is set, bits 0 and 5 must be clear -- so 0xE0, with bits 5 and 6 both set, is non-conformant. The corpus nevertheless requires the job to succeed and the bits to be written exactly as requested (224), because the operator may be mid-way through repairing a font and a tool that silently drops half of a two-checkbox edit is worse than one that obeys. The obligation the tool does have is to say so; that assertion needs the proposed warns check and is listed against this case in _proposed_checks.

<sub>covers E5 · authority: `judgement` · fixture: `recursive-vf`</sub>

### `bitflags.contradiction-regular-and-italic`

**REGULAR together with ITALIC is written as asked**

Bit 6 REGULAR ("Glyphs are in the standard weight/style for the font") and bit 0 ITALIC ("Font contains italic or oblique glyphs") are contradictory statements about the same glyphs, and the OS/2 specification makes them mutually exclusive. The requested value 0xC1 = 193 must still be written rather than silently sanitised, on the same reasoning as the REGULAR+BOLD case: the tool does not know which of the two the user meant, and guessing would produce a font that differs from the one asked for with no record of the substitution. A warning is the correct channel; see _proposed_checks.

<sub>covers E5 · authority: `judgement` · fixture: `recursive-vf`</sub>

### `bitflags.fsselection-bit0-clear`

**Unticking OS/2.fsSelection bit 0 leaves ITALIC clear**

Clearing a bit that is already clear must be a no-op on the whole field, not an excuse to rewrite it. The fixture is Recursive Sans Linear Light, an upright face whose fsSelection is 0xC0, so bit 0 ITALIC is already 0 and the OS/2 specification's description of bit 0 ("Font contains italic or oblique glyphs, otherwise they are upright") is already truthful. The output must therefore still be 0xC0 = 192, with bits 6 REGULAR and 7 USE_TYPO_METRICS untouched. This is the idempotence half of E3.

<sub>covers E1, E3 · authority: `slice-ui` · fixture: `recursive-vf`</sub>

### `bitflags.fsselection-bit0-set`

**Ticking OS/2.fsSelection bit 0 sets ITALIC**

The OpenType OS/2 specification defines fsSelection bit 0 ITALIC as "Font contains italic or oblique glyphs, otherwise they are upright", so the bit is a declaration about the glyphs and is exactly the kind of thing a slicing tool must let the operator restate after pinning a slant axis. The editor exposes this checkbox (E1), so ticking it must set that one bit and leave the rest of the 16-bit field as the font had it. The fixture's fsSelection is 0xC0 (bits 6 and 7), so the correct result is 0xC1 = 193. The output is spec-inconsistent because bit 6 REGULAR remains set alongside bit 0; that is deliberate here to keep this case about the single checkbox, and the contradiction itself is adjudicated by the bitflags.contradiction-* cases.

<sub>covers E1, E3 · authority: `slice-ui` · fixture: `recursive-vf`</sub>

### `bitflags.fsselection-bit5-clear`

**Unticking OS/2.fsSelection bit 5 leaves BOLD clear**

The fixture is a Light face with usWeightClass 300 and fsSelection 0xC0, so bit 5 BOLD is already 0, which is what the OS/2 specification's "Glyphs are emboldened" requires of a font whose glyphs are not emboldened. An unticked checkbox for an already-clear bit must leave the field at 192; producing any other value would mean the editor is writing state it invented rather than state the user expressed.

<sub>covers E1, E3 · authority: `slice-ui` · fixture: `recursive-vf`</sub>

### `bitflags.fsselection-bit5-set`

**Ticking OS/2.fsSelection bit 5 sets BOLD**

The OS/2 specification defines fsSelection bit 5 BOLD as "Glyphs are emboldened". A user who has just pinned a variable weight axis at its heavy end is the canonical reason this checkbox exists, since instancing sets usWeightClass from the pinned location but never touches the style bits. Ticking bit 5 must OR 0x20 into the existing 0xC0, giving 0xE0 = 224, and must not disturb bit 7 USE_TYPO_METRICS, which the editor does not expose.

<sub>covers E1, E3 · authority: `slice-ui` · fixture: `recursive-vf`</sub>

### `bitflags.fsselection-bit6-clear`

**Unticking OS/2.fsSelection bit 6 clears REGULAR, and only that bit**

Clearing REGULAR is a legitimate request when the operator is about to declare the sliced instance Bold or Italic instead, since the OS/2 specification makes bit 6 mutually exclusive with bits 0 and 5. What must not happen is collateral damage: the fixture's 0xC0 must become 0x80 = 128, retaining bit 7 USE_TYPO_METRICS, which the editor does not expose. Note that 128 is also what the original writes for an untouched editor, for the wrong reason (E4) -- here it is correct because the user asked for it.

<sub>covers E1, E3 · authority: `slice-ui` · fixture: `recursive-vf`</sub>

### `bitflags.fsselection-bit6-set`

**Ticking OS/2.fsSelection bit 6 sets REGULAR**

The OS/2 specification defines fsSelection bit 6 REGULAR as "Glyphs are in the standard weight/style for the font", and this fixture already declares itself Regular: its fsSelection is 0xC0, bits 6 and 7. A ticked bit-6 checkbox therefore asks for the state the font already has, and the output must still be 192. This case pins down that setting a bit is an assignment to 1, not a toggle; a toggle implementation would clear bit 6 here and produce 128.

<sub>covers E1, E3 · authority: `slice-ui` · fixture: `recursive-vf`</sub>

### `bitflags.fsselection-bit8-clear`

**Unticking OS/2.fsSelection bit 8 leaves WWS clear**

The fixture does not set bit 8, so it makes no WWS claim, and an unticked checkbox must leave that so: the field stays 192. The OS/2 specification ties bit 8 to whether name IDs 21 and 22 are needed, so a tool that spuriously set it would be asserting something about the name table it has not checked. Clearing an already-clear high bit must not smear into the low byte either.

<sub>covers E1, E3 · authority: `slice-ui` · fixture: `recursive-vf`</sub>

### `bitflags.fsselection-bit8-set`

**Ticking OS/2.fsSelection bit 8 sets WWS**

The OS/2 specification defines fsSelection bit 8 WWS as meaning the font "has 'name' table strings consistent with a weight/width/slope family without requiring use of name IDs 21 and 22". Slicing changes exactly the thing that claim is about -- the name records and the surviving design space -- so the operator must be able to assert or retract it. Setting bit 8 on the fixture's 0xC0 must give 0x1C0 = 448, which also proves the editor handles a bit above the low byte correctly.

<sub>covers E1, E3 · authority: `slice-ui` · fixture: `recursive-vf`</sub>

### `bitflags.italic-bit-does-not-change-italicangle`

**Setting ITALIC does not move post.italicAngle**

post.italicAngle is a measured angle in degrees counter-clockwise from vertical, which fontTools derives from the pinned slnt location; fsSelection bit 0 and macStyle bit 1 are style flags. Pinning slnt at 0 must leave italicAngle at 0 even when the user declares the instance italic, because an upright face declared italic is a name-and-style-map decision and inventing a slant angle for it would misreport the outlines. The same independence argument as the BOLD/usWeightClass pair, in the other table.

<sub>covers E3, G7 · authority: `spec` · fixture: `recursive-vf`</sub>

### `bitflags.macstyle-bit0-clear`

**Unticking head.macStyle bit 0 leaves BOLD clear**

The fixture's head.macStyle is 0, so bit 0 Bold is already clear and an unticked checkbox must leave the whole field at 0. The head specification requires macStyle bits 7 to 15 to be 0 and gives bits 2 to 6 specific meanings (underline, outline, shadow, condensed, extended), so a write that produced anything but 0 would be asserting styles the font does not have.

<sub>covers E2, E3 · authority: `slice-ui` · fixture: `recursive-vf`</sub>

### `bitflags.macstyle-bit0-set`

**Ticking head.macStyle bit 0 sets BOLD without touching OS/2**

The OpenType head specification defines macStyle bit 0 as "Bold (if set to 1)" and reserves bits 7 to 15, which "must be set to 0". The fixture's macStyle is 0, so ticking the bit-0 checkbox must produce exactly 1: no reserved bit invented, and bit 1 ITALIC left alone. It must also leave OS/2.fsSelection at 192, because macStyle and fsSelection are separate fields edited by separate checkboxes and a head edit is not licence to rewrite OS/2.

<sub>covers E2, E3 · authority: `slice-ui` · fixture: `recursive-vf`</sub>

### `bitflags.macstyle-bit1-clear`

**Unticking head.macStyle bit 1 leaves ITALIC clear**

The fixture is upright with macStyle 0 and post.italicAngle 0, so bit 1 Italic is correctly clear and must stay clear. Per the head specification bit 1 means "Italic (if set to 1)", a claim about the glyphs, and nothing in an unticked checkbox authorises changing it. The field must remain exactly 0.

<sub>covers E2, E3 · authority: `slice-ui` · fixture: `recursive-vf`</sub>

### `bitflags.macstyle-bit1-set`

**Ticking head.macStyle bit 1 sets ITALIC**

The head specification defines macStyle bit 1 as "Italic (if set to 1)". Ticking it on a font whose macStyle is 0 must give exactly 2, leaving bit 0 Bold clear and the reserved bits at 0. This is the head-table counterpart of fsSelection bit 0, and the two are required to agree; the agreement itself is the subject of the bitflags.consistent-* and bitflags.contradiction-* cases.

<sub>covers E2, E3 · authority: `slice-ui` · fixture: `recursive-vf`</sub>

### `bitflags.macstyle-edit-does-not-disturb-fsselection`

**Editing head.macStyle alone leaves the untouched OS/2 checkboxes alone**

A user who ticks only the head.macStyle Italic box has said nothing about OS/2.fsSelection, so the four fsSelection checkboxes are still showing whatever the font contains and must be written back unchanged: 192, with bit 6 REGULAR intact. The original collects all six checkbox states on every slice regardless of which the user touched, so it writes fsSelection 128 here and destroys the REGULAR declaration as a side effect of a head edit; it is expected to fail. The resulting output is also inconsistent under the head specification's requirement that macStyle bits 0 and 1 agree with fsSelection bits 5 and 0 -- deliberately so, since this case is about preservation and bitflags.contradiction-macstyle-italic-without-fsselection covers the warning.

<sub>covers A5, E3, E4 · authority: `spec` · fixture: `recursive-vf`</sub>

### `bitflags.slnt-pin-does-not-set-italic-bits`

**Pinning a slant axis does not set the ITALIC bits by itself**

fontTools' set_default_weight_width_slant writes post.italicAngle from the pinned slnt location -- here -15 -- but only setRibbiBits touches fsSelection and macStyle, and instantiateVariableFont calls it solely when updateFontNames is true, which Slice does not pass. Style bits are therefore the user's declaration, never an inference from geometry, which is right: an oblique instance is not automatically the family's Italic style, and the OS/2 specification ties bit 0 to a claim about the font rather than to an angle. With the editor untouched the output must keep fsSelection 192 and macStyle 0 while italicAngle becomes -15.

<sub>covers E4, G7 · authority: `fonttools` · fixture: `recursive-vf`</sub>

### `bitflags.two-axis-clear-is-absolute`

**An unticked box means 0 regardless of what the font had**

The mirror of the previous case, and the one that matters more, since clearing is how a user retracts a claim the font makes wrongly -- a Regular-marked face being sliced into a Bold, say. Every one of the six exposed bits must read 0 afterwards, on a fixture whose starting value this case does not assume. Bits the editor does not expose are out of scope here and are pinned down on recursive-vf, where their initial values are known.

<sub>covers E1, E2, E3 · authority: `slice-ui` · fixture: `two-axis`</sub>

### `bitflags.two-axis-set-is-absolute`

**A ticked box means 1 regardless of what the font had**

The editor's contract is assignment, not toggling: a ticked box means the bit is 1 in the output whatever it was in the input. Asserting only bit_set on a second fixture, whose fsSelection this case does not depend on, separates that contract from the recursive-vf cases that hard-code 0xC0. An implementation that XORed the checkbox state against the font's value would pass some recursive-vf cases by luck and fail here.

<sub>covers E1, E2, E3 · authority: `slice-ui` · fixture: `two-axis`</sub>

### `bitflags.unexposed-bit7-survives-a-clear`

**USE_TYPO_METRICS survives clearing an exposed bit**

The dangerous direction for an unexposed bit is a clear, because an implementation that assembles fsSelection from the six checkboxes rather than editing the font's value will zero everything it does not know about. Clearing bit 6 REGULAR must yield exactly 0x80 = 128: bit 7 USE_TYPO_METRICS still set, bits 0, 5 and 8 still clear. The OS/2 specification treats bit 7 as vertical-metrics policy that is independent of style classification, so no style edit may disturb it.

<sub>covers E3 · authority: `spec` · fixture: `recursive-vf`</sub>

### `bitflags.unexposed-bit7-survives-a-set`

**USE_TYPO_METRICS survives setting an exposed bit, in a static instance**

The fixture has fsSelection bit 7 USE_TYPO_METRICS set, and the OS/2 specification says that when it is set "it is strongly recommended that applications use OS/2.sTypoAscender - OS/2.sTypoDescender + OS/2.sTypoLineGap as the default line spacing". Dropping it silently changes line spacing in every application that honours it, so it is a layout regression, not a cosmetic one. The editor does not expose bit 7, so setting bit 5 BOLD must leave it set: 0xC0 becomes 0xE0 = 224. Pinning every axis at once makes the point on the static-instance path, where the most table rewriting happens.

<sub>covers E3, G1 · authority: `spec` · fixture: `recursive-vf`</sub>

### `bitflags.untouched-editor-preserves-bits-in-static-instance`

**An untouched editor preserves the REGULAR bit in a fully pinned instance**

Pinning every axis is the commonest use of the tool and produces the font most likely to be installed and style-linked, so it is exactly where losing fsSelection bit 6 REGULAR does the most damage. fontTools' instantiateVariableFont does not touch fsSelection or macStyle unless updateFontNames is passed, which the original does not pass, so any change seen here comes from the bit editor and not from instancing. The output must still be 192 with macStyle 0. The original writes 128 and is expected to fail.

<sub>covers A5, E4, G1 · authority: `spec` · fixture: `recursive-vf`</sub>

### `bitflags.untouched-editor-preserves-bits-into-woff2`

**Bit preservation is a property of the font, not of the container**

OS/2 and head are ordinary sfnt tables that WOFF2 transports unchanged, so the container the user asks for must have no bearing on the style bits. Writing the same untouched-editor job to WOFF2 must still yield fsSelection 192 with bit 6 REGULAR set. This guards against an implementation that reconstructs OS/2 on the compression path, and it separates a container bug from a bit-editor bug when the previous two cases fail.

<sub>covers A5, E4, H1 · authority: `spec` · fixture: `recursive-vf`</sub>

### `bitflags.untouched-editor-preserves-fsselection`

**An untouched Bit Flag Editor changes no bit at all**

This is the corrected form of the E4/A5 defect and the single most important case in this area. The fixture's OS/2.fsSelection is 0xC0: bit 6 REGULAR, which the OS/2 specification describes as "Glyphs are in the standard weight/style for the font", plus bit 7 USE_TYPO_METRICS. A user who slices an axis and never opens the bit editor has expressed no opinion about style classification, so the output must still read 192. The original unchecks all six boxes on load and writes that state, producing 128 -- a font that declares itself neither Regular nor Bold nor Italic, which leaves style-linking and the RIBBI style-map ambiguous: Windows and layout engines that pick a family member by the RIBBI bits have nothing to match, and the face can fall out of its own family grouping. The original is expected to fail this case.

<sub>covers A5, E4 · authority: `spec` · fixture: `recursive-vf`</sub>

### `bitflags.usweightclass-700-does-not-set-bold-bit`

**A heavy pinned weight does not set the BOLD bits by itself**

The converse of the previous case: pinning wght at 700 makes usWeightClass 700, but fsSelection bit 5 and macStyle bit 0 are declarations about the font's role in its family and only the user can make them. Many families ship a 700 face that is the family's Bold and many ship one that is a named weight in a larger set, and the OS/2 specification gives no rule for telling them apart from the number. With the editor untouched the output must keep fsSelection 192 and macStyle 0.

<sub>covers A5, E4, G7 · authority: `fonttools` · fixture: `recursive-vf`</sub>

## names

The nine `name` records the editor exposes, and what happens to the ones it does not. A font's names are how an operating system groups it into a family, so losing one is not cosmetic.

Covers claims: D1, D2, D3, D4, D5, D6, G1, G10, G2, G4, G5, G7.

### `names.d1.nine-editable-records-are-written`

**All nine editable rows reach the output as 3/1/1033 records**

The editor exposes exactly nine name IDs — 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 16, 17, 21, 22 — and the name specification says of them that “the key information for this table for Microsoft platforms relates to the use of name IDs 1, 2, 4, 16 and 17” and that “fonts should include all of these strings for the broadest application compatibility”. A slicer that offered a row and then dropped what was typed into it would be worse than not offering the row. This is the baseline for the whole area: nine cells in, nine records out, each holding exactly the typed string.

<sub>covers D1, D2, D3, D4 · authority: `slice-ui` · fixture: `recursive-vf`</sub>

### `names.d1.nine-rows-on-a-font-that-already-has-them`

**Editing all nine rows overwrites the records the font already had**

The previous case creates records that were absent; this one replaces records that were present, which is a different path in any implementation that treats 16, 17, 21 and 22 as optional. Name ID 17 “must be unique within a particular typographic family”, so an implementation that appended a second 3/1/1033 record instead of replacing the first would leave the table with two competing typographic subfamily names. Exactly one record per key must come out, which is why the case also counts them: two records for ID 17, the edited English one and the untouched German one.

<sub>covers D1, D4 · authority: `slice-ui` · fixture: `named-instances`</sub>

### `names.d2.editor-reads-the-english-record`

**With the editor untouched the English strings are written back, not the German ones**

The fixture’s German name ID 1 deliberately differs from its English one, so this case can tell which record an implementation loaded into its cells. Since the editor reads 3/1/1033 and always writes IDs 1, 2, 3, 4 and 6 back, an untouched slice must reproduce the English strings; had it read 3/1/1031 it would write “FixtureNamedInstances Deutsch” into the English record and silently rename the font for English users. The specification’s warning that applications “might display incorrect strings ... if strings for the current platform are not included” is exactly why the localisations must not be conflated.

<sub>covers D2, D3 · authority: `slice-ui` · fixture: `named-instances`</sub>

### `names.d2.macintosh-records-survive-a-slice`

**A font with Macintosh platform records keeps every one of them**

Platform 1 records are a legitimate part of the table — the specification lists platform ID 1 as valid in the name table and notes that “many newer platforms can use strings intended for different platforms if a font does not include strings for that platform”. Nothing about narrowing a design space invalidates a Macintosh string, so all of the fixture’s Mac records must be present and unchanged after a full pin with the name editor untouched. The encoding check matters because “strings for the Macintosh platform (platform ID 1) use platform-specific single- or double-byte encodings”: a tool that rewrote them as UTF-16BE would leave records no consumer can read.

<sub>covers D2, G10 · authority: `spec` · fixture: `named-instances`</sub>

### `names.d2.no-record-is-invented-on-another-platform`

**Creating name ID 16 creates one record, not one per platform**

two-axis has Macintosh and Windows English records for IDs 1 to 6 but no ID 16 anywhere, so typing a typographic family name must produce exactly one new record, on the key the editor owns. An implementation that helpfully mirrored the edit onto platform 1 would be inventing data, and would have to encode arbitrary user text in a “platform-specific single- or double-byte encoding” that in general cannot represent it. The set of platform keys in the output must match the set in the input.

<sub>covers D2, D4 · authority: `slice-ui` · fixture: `two-axis`</sub>

### `names.d2.non-english-windows-records-survive-a-slice`

**German Windows records are preserved when the English ones are edited**

The name table exists to hold “multilingual strings”, and the specification’s whole design is that “later, the font can be localized and the strings translated or added”. A localisation is not derivable from the English string and cannot be regenerated, so losing one is unrecoverable. Editing the English family and subfamily must leave all four German records exactly as they were, including the two that carry U+00FC and U+00DC — characters that survive a UTF-16BE round trip but not a naive Latin-1 or ASCII re-encode, which is why the case also pins the encoding the specification demands for platform 3.

<sub>covers D2 · authority: `spec` · fixture: `named-instances`</sub>

### `names.d2.only-windows-english-is-written`

**Editing name ID 1 changes the 3/1/1033 record and no other**

The editor’s contract is one localisation: Windows, Unicode BMP, English (US). The specification blesses that key — “when building a Unicode font for Windows, the platform ID should be 3 and the encoding ID should be 1” — but it also treats every other record as an independent string in its own language and encoding, and a tool cannot translate the user’s text into German or re-encode it for Mac Roman. Writing the edit anywhere else would corrupt or mistranslate those records, so the Macintosh and German name ID 1 records must come out exactly as they went in, and there must still be three of them.

<sub>covers D2 · authority: `slice-ui` · fixture: `named-instances`</sub>

### `names.d2.records-remain-sorted`

**The output name table is still in the order the specification requires**

The specification is explicit: “name records must be sorted first by platform ID, then by platform-specific encoding ID, then by language ID, and then by name ID.” Editing the table both adds and removes records, and an implementation that appends new ones to the end of the array, or leaves a hole where a removed one was, produces a table that violates that requirement even though every string in it is correct. The case is run on an input that both adds records (17 on the Mac platform is absent, 16 and 17 are rewritten) and removes them (21 and 22 are cleared).

<sub>covers D2, D4 · authority: `spec` · fixture: `named-instances`</sub>

### `names.d3.blank-mandatory-cells-still-write-records`

**Clearing rows 1, 2, 3, 4 and 6 leaves five empty records, not five absent ones**

Name IDs 1, 2, 4 and 6 are the strings every platform looks up first, and the specification says fonts “should include all of these strings for the broadest application compatibility”. Deleting them would leave a font that names itself nowhere; writing whatever the user typed, including nothing, at least keeps the required records present and makes the emptiness visible to a validator rather than turning it into a missing record that consumers paper over differently. Verified with fontTools 4.62.1 that a zero-length 3/1/1033 record survives a save and reload as a present, empty string.

<sub>covers D3 · authority: `slice-ui` · fixture: `two-axis`</sub>

### `names.d3.cleared-family-is-empty-not-absent`

**A cleared family-name cell yields a present record whose string is empty**

This is the sharp edge of the empty-versus-absent distinction, isolated on the single most important record. Name ID 1 is “the name the user sees” in the specification’s own worked example, and the rule for IDs 1 to 6 is the opposite of the rule for 16 to 22: the same empty cell means “write an empty string” here and “delete the record” there. A checker must be able to tell the two states apart, so the case asserts both that the record exists and that it is empty.

<sub>covers D3, D4 · authority: `slice-ui` · fixture: `recursive-vf`</sub>

### `names.d3.names-are-not-regenerated-from-the-pinned-location`

**Slicing to a different weight does not rewrite the family and subfamily names**

fontTools can regenerate name records from STAT axis values, but only when asked: instantiateVariableFont’s updateFontNames defaults to False and the original does not pass it. Verified with fontTools 4.62.1 that pinning wght=1000 leaves name ID 1 saying “Recursive Sans Linear Light” while OS/2.usWeightClass becomes 1000. That mismatch is exactly why a Name Editor exists, and resolving it must stay the user’s decision: the specification’s four-style rule means the right name ID 1 for an ExtraBlack cut is a judgement about family grouping — “the Font Family name for the Arial Black font is Arial Black” — not something a slicer can derive.

<sub>covers D3, G7 · authority: `fonttools` · fixture: `recursive-vf`</sub>

### `names.d3.untouched-editor-preserves-the-five`

**An untouched name editor writes the font's own strings back unchanged**

Because the five mandatory rows are loaded from the font and then always written, doing nothing must be a no-op on those records. Any drift here — a trailing space, a re-encoding, a value picked up from another platform — would mean the editor cannot safely be left alone, which is the property nearly every other case in this area rests on. The expected strings are the ones read out of the fixture with fontTools 4.62.1.

<sub>covers D3, D5 · authority: `slice-ui` · fixture: `recursive-vf`</sub>

### `names.d4.blank-optional-row-on-a-font-without-it`
