**Blank rows 16, 17, 21 and 22 on a font that never had them produce nothing**

two-axis has none of the four optional records. Blank cells must therefore be a no-op: not a deletion of something absent, and above all not the creation of four empty records. An empty ID 16 would be worse than none at all, because “if name ID 16 is absent, then name ID 1 is considered to be the typographic family name” — the fallback only fires when the record is genuinely absent.

<sub>covers D4 · authority: `slice-ui` · fixture: `two-axis`</sub>

### `names.d4.clearing-16-does-not-touch-other-languages`

**Deleting the typographic family name removes the 3/1/1033 record only**

The editor’s scope is one localisation, so its deletions are scoped the same way and the German name ID 16 must survive. The result is a table whose English typographic family name is absent while its German one is present — internally odd, but the alternative is a tool that silently deletes localisations the user never saw and cannot restore. Recording the consequence here makes it a deliberate part of the contract rather than an accident, and gives the D5 adjudication the full picture of what scoped deletion produces.

<sub>covers D4, D2 · authority: `slice-ui` · fixture: `named-instances`</sub>

### `names.d4.clearing-16-removes-only-16`

**Clearing row 16 deletes the typographic family record and leaves 17, 21 and 22**

For IDs 16, 17, 21 and 22 an empty cell means “this font should not have this record”, and the specification makes absence a defined state with a defined fallback: “if name ID 16 is absent, then name ID 1 is considered to be the typographic family name.” An empty string would instead advertise a typographic family called nothing, which no fallback rescues. The other three records must be untouched, because the user cleared one cell and not four.

<sub>covers D4 · authority: `slice-ui` · fixture: `named-instances`</sub>

### `names.d4.clearing-21-and-22-removes-both`

**Clearing the two WWS rows deletes both records and leaves 16 and 17**

IDs 21 and 22 are conditional by design: they are “used to provide a WWS-conformant family name in case the entries for IDs 16 and 17 do not conform to the WWS model”, and the specification adds that “if bit 8 of the OS/2 fsSelection field is set, a WWS Family Name entry should not be needed and should not be included”. A user who slices a font down to a WWS-conformant cut therefore has a real reason to delete them, and the tool must delete rather than blank: an empty ID 21 would still count as “an entry for this ID is included”, which the specification says must correlate with fsSelection bit 8 being clear.

<sub>covers D4 · authority: `spec` · fixture: `named-instances`</sub>

### `names.d4.clearing-all-four-optional-rows`

**Clearing 16, 17, 21 and 22 removes all four when the user asks for it**

This is the output the original produces for every font it touches, but here it is produced because the user deliberately emptied four cells, which makes it correct rather than accidental. The distinction is the whole of D5: the same bytes are right when requested and wrong when imposed. Keeping this case next to the D5 cases makes the corpus say plainly that the deletion mechanism is fine and only its default is not.

<sub>covers D4 · authority: `slice-ui` · fixture: `named-instances`</sub>

### `names.d4.empty-versus-absent-in-one-output`

**The same empty cell leaves an empty record at ID 4 and no record at ID 21**

This case exists to make the empty-versus-absent distinction impossible to miss: two cells are cleared in one run and the outcomes are opposite. ID 4 stays because the full font name is one of the strings the specification says fonts “should include ... for the broadest application compatibility”; ID 21 goes because it is conditional and its absence is a defined state. An implementation that handles the empty string uniformly will fail exactly one of these two checks, which is the diagnosis the case is built to deliver.

<sub>covers D3, D4 · authority: `slice-ui` · fixture: `named-instances`</sub>

### `names.d4.typographic-names-written-when-non-empty`

**Non-empty rows 16 and 17 create records on a font that had none**

recursive-vf has no name ID 16 or 17 on any platform, so this exercises creation rather than replacement. The specification recommends exactly this for a sliced family member: “for extended typographic families that includes fonts other than the four basic styles ... it is strongly recommended that name IDs 16 and 17 be used in fonts to create an extended, typographic grouping.” A user pinning one cut out of a five-axis variable font is producing precisely such a member, so the editor must be able to add these records — and must not add 21 and 22, which were left blank.

<sub>covers D4 · authority: `spec` · fixture: `recursive-vf`</sub>

### `names.d4.whitespace-is-not-empty`

**A row containing a single space is written, not treated as cleared**

The boundary between “write it” and “delete it” is an exact comparison against the empty string, so a cell holding one space falls on the write side. Nothing in the name specification forbids a string of whitespace, and the two candidate behaviours differ materially — one output has an ID 16 record and the other does not — so the corpus has to say which. Trimming would be a silent reinterpretation of what the user typed, the same fault the corpus rejects in B8; if a future version wants to refuse whitespace-only input it should refuse it out loud, not guess.

<sub>covers D4 · authority: `judgement` · fixture: `named-instances`</sub>

### `names.d5.editing-one-row-does-not-strip-the-other-four`

**Editing the family name leaves the typographic and WWS names alone**

This is the shape the defect takes in ordinary use: the user changes one string and four unrelated records vanish. Under the corrected behaviour the four optional rows were loaded with the font’s own values, so writing them back is a no-op and only name ID 1 changes. The specification’s worked examples for extended families set IDs 1, 2, 16, 17, 21 and 22 together as one coherent set; a tool that lets a user retitle a font while silently discarding four of the six is not editing that set, it is truncating it. The original is expected to fail this case.

<sub>covers D5, D3, D4 · authority: `spec` · fixture: `named-instances`</sub>

### `names.d5.loaded-value-can-still-be-replaced`

**Loading 16 and 17 into the editor does not make them read-only**

The fix for D5 is to load all nine rows rather than five; a careless fix that loaded them but then refused to overwrite would trade one defect for another. Name ID 17 “must be unique within a particular typographic family”, so a user slicing a new cut out of a family very often does have to change it. Loading and editing must compose: the loaded value appears in the cell, the typed value wins, and the German record is not dragged along with it.

<sub>covers D5, D4, D1 · authority: `slice-ui` · fixture: `named-instances`</sub>

### `names.d5.no-typographic-names-are-invented`

**A font with no 16, 17, 21 or 22 does not acquire them**

Loading all nine rows means loading four empty ones when the font has no such records, and the correct output then has no such records either. The specification’s Times New Roman example shows a font that legitimately omits all four — “Preferred Family. No name string present, since it is the same as name ID 1” — so inventing them, for instance by copying ID 1 into ID 16, would add claims the font never made. recursive-vf is exactly such a font: its table holds only IDs 0 to 6 and 269 to 414, verified with fontTools 4.62.1.

<sub>covers D5, D4 · authority: `slice-ui` · fixture: `recursive-vf`</sub>

### `names.d5.other-language-typographic-names-are-not-the-fix`

**The German typographic names survive, which is what makes the English loss inconsistent**

The original’s deletion is scoped to 3/1/1033, so a font carrying typographic names in more than one language comes out with the English pair missing and the German pair intact. That is diagnostic rather than mitigating: the specification treats the localisations as translations of one logical string, so a table asserting a German typographic family and no English one is self-contradictory, and consumers that fall back across languages may show German to English users. Both implementations should pass this case; it exists so the D5 adjudication sees the whole of what the original produces.

<sub>covers D5, D2 · authority: `slice-ui` · fixture: `named-instances`</sub>

### `names.d5.typographic-names-survive-a-partial-slice`

**A partial slice that leaves a variable font also keeps 16, 17, 21 and 22**

The defect is in the name editor, not the instancer, so it applies just as much when the output is still variable — and the stakes are higher there, because the specification observes that “variable fonts can include a large number of named instances, each of which will use a shared typographic family name (name ID 16)”. Pinning wdth leaves five wght instances in fvar, and deleting ID 16 would leave all five without the family name they are meant to share. The original is expected to fail this case.

<sub>covers D5, G2 · authority: `spec` · fixture: `named-instances`</sub>

### `names.d5.untouched-editor-preserves-typographic-names`

**Slicing without touching the name editor keeps name IDs 16 and 17**

This is the corrected behaviour for the corpus’s largest suspected defect: the original never loads IDs 16, 17, 21 or 22 into the editor, so all four cells are blank, and D4’s rule then deletes all four from every font it touches. The specification makes those records load-bearing for a fixture like this one, which has eight named instances: name ID 1 “should be shared among at most four fonts that differ only in weight or style (italic/oblique)”, whereas name ID 16’s “typographic family grouping doesn’t impose any constraints on the number of faces within it”, and “if name ID 16 is absent, then name ID 1 is considered to be the typographic family name”. Delete 16 and 17 from a family with more than four styles and every face falls back on the four-style ID 1 / ID 2 grouping, so the fifth and later styles can only be style-linked by being split into separate families — which is why the specification warns that applications assuming that grouping “are likely to provide a poor user experience with variable fonts”. The original is expected to fail this case.

<sub>covers D5, D4, D1 · authority: `spec` · fixture: `named-instances`</sub>

### `names.d5.untouched-editor-preserves-wws-names`

**Slicing without touching the name editor keeps name IDs 21 and 22**

The same defect strips the WWS pair. IDs 21 and 22 are there for a face whose ID 17 “includes qualifiers for some attribute other than weight, width or slope”, and the specification ties them to a bit: “if an entry for this ID is included, bit 8 should not be set”. Deleting ID 21 while leaving fsSelection bit 8 clear leaves a font that is neither declared WWS-conformant nor annotated with a WWS name, so a layout engine has nothing to group it by. The original is expected to fail this case.

<sub>covers D5, D4 · authority: `spec` · fixture: `named-instances`</sub>

### `names.d6.version-and-other-non-editable-records-are-preserved`

**Name ID 5 is read-only, and records outside the nine are carried through**

The editor reads name ID 5 only to show a version in the status bar; there is no row for it, so the string must survive, and so must every other name ID outside the nine. The specification requires ID 5 to “begin with the pattern Version <number>.<number>” and notes that “the first such match in the string can be used by installation software to compare font versions”, so blanking or bumping it would change how installers treat the file. ID 0 is the vendor’s copyright notice, which no font tool has any business rewriting. The case edits five rows the editor does own, to show that doing so perturbs neither.

<sub>covers D6, D1 · authority: `slice-ui` · fixture: `recursive-vf`</sub>

### `names.g10.axis-name-survives-its-own-axis-being-pinned`

**The Weight axis name record survives even though wght was pinned away**

This is the subtlety that makes “drop unused” the wrong summary. fvar is gone, so nothing in fvar references name ID 271 Weight any more — but STAT keeps its design axis records in full, and each of those records must carry an AxisNameID, so 271 is still referenced and must stay. Verified with fontTools 4.62.1: all five axis-name records, 269 to 273, survive a full pin of recursive-vf. An implementation that pruned by walking fvar alone would delete records STAT still points at, leaving a STAT table with dangling name IDs.

<sub>covers G10, G5 · authority: `fonttools` · fixture: `recursive-vf`</sub>

### `names.g10.deleting-a-name-does-not-break-a-surviving-reference`

**After a partial slice every fvar and STAT name reference still resolves**

Pruning guards against orphaned records; this checks the opposite fault, a live reference to a record that is gone. It is reachable in practice, and this fixture shows how: its default instance record uses subfamilyNameID 2, which the fvar specification explicitly permits — “values of 2 or 17 can be used” — so an instance can point at a name ID the name editor owns, and clearing row 17 on a font that used 17 there would leave fvar pointing at nothing. The case slices partially so that fvar and STAT both survive, and clears the two WWS rows, which nothing references, to establish that a legitimate deletion leaves every reference intact.

<sub>covers G10, D4 · authority: `spec` · fixture: `named-instances`</sub>

### `names.g10.editing-does-not-resurrect-pruned-records`

**Editing the name table does not bring back instance names the slice removed**

The complement of the exact-set case: an implementation that rebuilt the name table from the source font in order to apply the user’s edits would restore the 128 instance-name records pruning had just removed, inflating the output and orphaning every one of them. The edits must be applied to the sliced table in place. The surviving set is the one verified with fontTools 4.62.1 for this location, and it must not grow because two cells were typed into.

<sub>covers G10, D3 · authority: `fonttools` · fixture: `recursive-vf`</sub>

### `names.g10.exact-surviving-name-ids-after-a-full-pin`

**Exactly sixteen name IDs remain after pinning Recursive to Sans Linear Regular**

The pruning rule is not “drop what nothing references” but “drop the IDs that fvar or STAT referenced before and no longer do”, applied only above 255. Verified with fontTools 4.62.1 at MONO=0, CASL=0, wght=400, slnt=0, CRSV=0.5: the survivors are exactly IDs 0 to 6, the five STAT design-axis names 269 to 273, and the four STAT axis values that match the pinned location — 402 Sans, 404 Linear, 406 Regular, 413 Upright. Stating the whole set rather than a few members is what lets the case catch over-pruning and under-pruning with one assertion.

<sub>covers G10, G5 · authority: `fonttools` · fixture: `recursive-vf`</sub>

### `names.g10.exact-surviving-name-ids-on-named-instances`

**Pinning wght=700 keeps only the Bold and Normal value names**

The same rule on the fixture the roster designates for name pruning, where the numbering is small enough to read. Verified with fontTools 4.62.1: pinning wght=700, wdth=100 leaves IDs 1 to 6, the two axis names 256 and 257, the STAT weight value 263 Bold, and the STAT width value 274 Normal — which survives despite being flagged elidable, because elision affects how a name is displayed, not whether the axis value matches. All eight instance names and their PostScript names go, as do the Condensed and Expanded value names at 273 and 275.

<sub>covers G10, G4, G5 · authority: `fonttools` · fixture: `named-instances`</sub>

### `names.g10.full-pin-can-prune-nothing-at-all`

**A font with no named instances loses no name records when every axis is pinned**

two-axis declares both axes but no fvar instances, so the only name IDs above 255 are the two axis names, and STAT keeps its design axis records in full (G5) with their AxisNameID intact. Verified with fontTools 4.62.1: pinning wght=400, wdth=100 removes fvar and removes not one name record. This is the counterexample to reading G10 as “a full pin strips the name table” — what gets pruned depends entirely on what STAT still points at.

<sub>covers G10, G1, G5 · authority: `fonttools` · fixture: `two-axis`</sub>

### `names.g10.instance-names-pruned-on-full-pin`

**Pinning every axis drops the name records that only named fvar instances**

With no fvar left, the 64 instance subfamily and PostScript name records reference nothing, and the specification reserves “name IDs 256 to 32767, inclusive ... for font-specific names”, so these strings are private to the font and worthless once their referrer is gone. Verified with fontTools 4.62.1: pinning MONO=0, CASL=0, wght=400, slnt=0, CRSV=0.5 removes IDs 274 through 401 apart from those still reachable from STAT. The user-facing records at IDs 1 to 6 are untouched by pruning.

<sub>covers G10, G1 · authority: `fonttools` · fixture: `recursive-vf`</sub>

### `names.g10.layout-feature-label-survives`

**A stylistic-set UI label is not pruned, even though fvar and STAT never referenced it**

This is the case that shows the rule is not “drop every name ID nothing in fvar or STAT points at”. The specification reserves “name IDs 256 to 32767, inclusive ... for font-specific names such as those referenced by a font’s layout features”, and a GSUB FeatureParams UINameID is exactly such a reference; fontTools prunes only IDs that were variation-referenced before the operation and are not after, so a label that was never in that set is never a candidate. Deleting it would leave the ss01 feature pointing at nothing and strip the name a user interface shows for the feature. Note that the listed no_dangling_name_ids check would wrongly fail this output, which is why name_references_resolve is proposed above and used here instead.

<sub>covers G10 · authority: `spec` · fixture: `named-instances`</sub>

### `names.g10.partial-slice-keeps-the-instances-it-still-has`

**A partial slice prunes only the instance names whose instances went away**

Pinning MONO, CASL, slnt and CRSV while leaving wght free reduces Recursive’s 64 named instances to the 8 upright Sans Linear ones, and only the other 56 may lose their names. Verified with fontTools 4.62.1: IDs 338/339, 346/347 and 394/395 — Sans Linear Light, Sans Linear and Sans Linear ExtraBlack with their PostScript names — survive, while the Mono (274) and Sans Casual (342) instance names are gone. The surviving fvar records must still resolve, since the specification requires an instance’s subfamilyNameID to name “entries in the name table”; recursive-vf carries no layout-feature labels, so on this fixture the stronger statement holds too, that every ID above 255 is reachable from fvar or STAT.

<sub>covers G10, G4, G2 · authority: `fonttools` · fixture: `recursive-vf`</sub>

### `names.g10.pruning-happens-before-the-name-edits`

**Records written by the editor are not pruned by the instancer that ran before them**

Slicing runs first and the name edits second, so nothing the user typed can be swept away by pruning; the ordering matters because a tool that edited first and instanced second would lose any newly written ID above 255. All nine editable IDs are 255 or below and so are safe either way, but the case fixes the observable end state: after a full pin the edited strings are present and the pruned instance names are still gone. Verified with fontTools 4.62.1 at MONO=1, CASL=1, wght=700, slnt=-15, CRSV=1, where the surviving IDs above 255 are 269 to 273, 403, 409 and 414.

<sub>covers G10, D3, D4 · authority: `slice-ui` · fixture: `recursive-vf`</sub>

### `names.g10.reserved-name-ids-are-never-pruned`

**Name IDs 255 and below are outside the pruning rule entirely**

The specification partitions the number space: “name IDs 26 to 255, inclusive, are reserved for future standard names. Name IDs 256 to 32767, inclusive, are reserved for font-specific names such as those referenced by a font’s layout features.” Only the second range can be private to fvar or STAT, so only it can be pruned; a standard name ID means the same thing to every consumer whether or not a table points at it. Verified with fontTools 4.62.1: adding IDs 16, 17, 21 and 22 to recursive-vf and then pinning every axis leaves all four in place, along with 0 and 5 — so any loss of those records is attributable to the name editor and not to the instancer.

<sub>covers G10, D4 · authority: `spec` · fixture: `recursive-vf`</sub>

### `names.g10.stat-axis-values-outside-the-slice-lose-their-names`

**STAT axis values dropped by the slice take their name records with them**

STAT axis values whose coordinates fall outside the new limits are dropped (G5), and their ValueNameID records then have no referrer left, so they go too. Verified with fontTools 4.62.1: pinning wght=400 keeps 406 Regular and removes 405 Light, 411 Black and 412 ExtraBlack, while pinning CASL=0 keeps 404 Linear and removes 403 Mono. Keeping them would leave orphaned strings in the file; dropping the wrong ones would leave STAT pointing at a name record that is not there.

<sub>covers G10, G5 · authority: `fonttools` · fixture: `recursive-vf`</sub>

### `names.postscript.invalid-value-is-not-silently-repaired`

**A PostScript name containing a space is written unchanged rather than mangled**

A space is outside the printable-ASCII subset the specification allows for name ID 6, so this input is not conformant — but the editor performs no validation, and of the two available behaviours, “write it as typed” and “quietly rewrite it”, the second is strictly worse: the user ships a name they never chose and never saw. Refusing the job would also be defensible, and if the project adopts that it should be recorded as a new claim in the behaviour map rather than arrived at by one implementation guessing. Until then the contract is verbatim, and complaining about the value is a validator’s job.

<sub>covers D1, D3 · authority: `judgement` · fixture: `two-axis`</sub>

### `names.postscript.written-verbatim`

**A valid PostScript name is written exactly as typed**

Name ID 6 is the most constrained of the nine: “when translated to ASCII, the name string must be no longer than 63 characters and restricted to the printable ASCII subset, codes 33 to 126, except for the 10 characters ‘[’, ‘]’, ‘(’, ‘)’, ‘{’, ‘}’, ‘<’, ‘>’, ‘/’, ‘%’”. A conforming value must therefore pass through untouched — no case folding, no truncation, no normalisation — because the string “is used to invoke a PostScript language font that corresponds to this OpenType font” and any alteration breaks that lookup.

<sub>covers D1, D3 · authority: `spec` · fixture: `two-axis`</sub>

### `names.unicode.astral-plane-round-trips`

**Characters outside the BMP survive as UTF-16 surrogate pairs**

Windows encoding ID 1 is named “Unicode BMP”, but the storage format is UTF-16BE, which encodes supplementary characters as surrogate pairs; verified with fontTools 4.62.1, U+1D11E and U+1F600 are stored as d834 dd1e and d83d de00 and decode back unchanged. What the case tests is that the tool neither truncates at the BMP boundary nor splits a pair, either of which would leave lone surrogates in the string storage and a string no decoder can recover. Whether a font ought to carry such a name is a separate question from whether an editor may silently corrupt what the user typed.

<sub>covers D2, D3 · authority: `spec` · fixture: `two-axis`</sub>

### `names.unicode.non-ascii-does-not-leak-onto-the-mac-platform`

**A non-ASCII edit is not mirrored onto a Macintosh Roman record**

This is where the single-localisation rule earns its keep. Macintosh platform strings “use platform-specific single- or double-byte encodings according to the specified encoding ID”, and Mac Roman cannot represent most of this string, so any implementation that mirrored the edit onto 1/0/0 would have to corrupt it or fail. The Windows record takes the new text; the Mac record keeps its old text, still in mac_roman.

<sub>covers D2 · authority: `spec` · fixture: `named-instances`</sub>

### `names.unicode.non-ascii-round-trips`

**Non-ASCII text typed into a name cell comes back unchanged**

For the key the editor writes, the specification is unambiguous: outside the code-page encodings 3, 4 and 5, “all string data for platform 3 must be encoded in UTF-16BE”, which covers the whole Basic Multilingual Plane, so Latin accents, Greek and CJK are all representable and must survive. Verified with fontTools 4.62.1: setting this string on 3/1/1033, saving and reloading returns it unchanged, stored as UTF-16BE. A tool that encoded to Latin-1 or fell back to ASCII would mangle names for most of the world’s scripts.

<sub>covers D2, D3 · authority: `spec` · fixture: `two-axis`</sub>

## outlines-containers

The glyphs themselves, the removal of overlapping contours, and the file formats the result can be written in.

Covers claims: A3, G12, G13, G14, G2, G8, H1, H2.

### `cff.advances-match-source`

**A CFF2 instance has the advances the source has at that location**

CFF2 has no `gvar`-style per-glyph metrics, so advances come from `hmtx` plus `HVAR`, and fontTools notes in the instancer that HVAR handling for CFF2 is incomplete (`# TODO(anthrotype) Add support for HVAR/VVAR in CFF2`, `varLib/instancer/__init__.py:1103`), with the metrics updated by a separate path (:1124). That makes this the CFF branch's most likely silent failure: correct outlines at wrong widths. Advances are integers in `hmtx`, so half a unit is the whole rounding budget.

<sub>covers G13 · authority: `fonttools` · fixture: `cff2-vf`</sub>

### `cff.extension-does-not-convert-outlines`

**Typing .ttf for a CFF font does not invent TrueType outlines**

Converting cubic CFF charstrings to quadratic `glyf` contours is a lossy re-drawing with its own error tolerance, and it is not what H1 describes: the extension selects the container, and `.ttf` and `.otf` are the same container. Silently producing approximated outlines because of a filename would be exactly the 'silent mangling' the corpus rejects — the user asked for a container, not a redraw. The output must remain a CFF-flavoured sfnt with no `glyf` table, and if an implementation believes the filename must be honoured, the only acceptable alternative is refusing the job, not converting.

<sub>covers H1, A3 · authority: `judgement` · fixture: `cff2-vf`</sub>

### `cff.partial-instance-stays-variable`

**Restricting an axis on a CFF2 font leaves a variable CFF2 font**

CFF2 carries its variation data in the charstrings' `blend` operators and the table's own ItemVariationStore, so narrowing an axis means rewriting blends and re-tenting the store rather than deleting a `gvar`. An implementation that handles the fully-pinned case by throwing the variation data away will produce a font that is either static when the user asked for variable, or variable with a store that no longer matches its blends. Requiring `fvar` and `CFF2` to both survive, and the outlines to be right at three sampled weights, is what distinguishes real partial instancing from deletion. The fixture's `wght` axis is 400/400/900 -- the default sits at the minimum, as it does in Recursive -- so 400:700 contains the default as B7 requires, and the restricted axis comes out 400/400/700.

<sub>covers G2, G13, A3 · authority: `fonttools` · fixture: `cff2-vf`</sub>

### `cff.remove-overlaps-preserves-filled-region`

**Overlap removal on a CFF font preserves the filled region**

CFF is the format where overlap removal is not merely an optimization: the Type 2 charstring specification says that overlapping subpaths are not permitted and that outlines must be non-overlapping for correct rendering, and PostScript interpreters fill CFF outlines with the non-zero rule but were never designed for self-intersection. fontTools reflects this by removing overlaps as part of any CFF2-to-CFF downgrade, 'as CFF does not support overlaps but CFF2 does' (`varLib/instancer/__init__.py`). The invariant is the same as for glyf — the filled region must not move — but the tolerance is tighter at half a unit, because CFF charstrings store fractional coordinates and the merged path is not forced onto the integer grid (fontTools uses `noRound` for the CFF path in `ttLib/removeOverlaps.py`). **The original never removes overlaps** (G14) and is expected to fail.

<sub>covers G14 · authority: `spec` · fixture: `cff2-vf` · **the original does not have this feature**</sub>

### `cff.static-instance-is-valid`

**A CFF2 variable font pinned on every axis yields a valid static CFF font**

A tool asked to do something it cannot must refuse clearly rather than write a mangled font — the adjudicated verdict on B8 in this project — and for CFF2 the mangled outcome is concrete: charstrings still carrying `blend` operators in a font whose variation store has been removed, which the OpenType CFF2 specification makes meaningless because `blend` is defined only against an ItemVariationStore. But refusal is not required here, because fontTools 4.62.1 does implement CFF2 instancing: `instantiateCFF2` (`varLib/instancer/__init__.py:649`) is dispatched whenever `"CFF2" in varfont` (:1747), so the original, which delegates wholesale to `instantiateVariableFont`, is expected to succeed. By the corpus rule that a case the original passes this implementation must also pass, the expectation is success with correct outlines; an implementation that genuinely cannot do this must emit an error naming CFF2, never a font.

<sub>covers A3, G13 · authority: `fonttools` · fixture: `cff2-vf`</sub>

### `cff.woff-container-wraps-cff-sfnt`

**A CFF font can be written into a WOFF container**

WOFF wraps any sfnt, whatever outline format it holds; the WOFF 1.0 specification is explicit that the format is outline-agnostic and preserves the sfntVersion of the wrapped font. So the choice of container and the choice of outline format are independent, and this case is the one that proves an implementation has not conflated 'WOFF' with 'compressed TrueType'. The outlines must survive the wrapper exactly, since WOFF adds nothing but compression.

<sub>covers H1, A3 · authority: `spec` · fixture: `cff2-vf`</sub>

### `container.composites-survive-woff2`

**Composite glyphs survive the WOFF2 glyf transform intact**

The WOFF2 glyf transform encodes composite glyph data in its own stream, separate from the simple-glyph point streams, so composites are the part of the transform most likely to be reconstructed wrongly. A decoder that loses a component's scale or its ARGS_ARE_XY_VALUES flag produces a glyph that still parses and still has the right component count but draws in the wrong place, which only an outline comparison catches. The fixture's two-deep nesting means an error in the inner composite propagates and is visible in the outer one too.

<sub>covers A3, H1 · authority: `spec` · fixture: `composites`</sub>

### `container.read-otf`

**An OTF (CFF-flavoured sfnt) input is accepted**

A3 claims all four of TrueType, CFF, WOFF and WOFF2 are readable because `TTFont` reads all four, and the open dialog offers `.otf`. Accepting `.otf` in the file filter and then failing on the file would be a broken promise made by the interface itself. `cff2-vf` is the roster's only CFF-flavoured sfnt, so it is the fixture that exercises the OTTO branch of the reader; this case asserts only that the font is read and produces a font, with the CFF-specific questions handled in the `cff.*` cases.

<sub>covers A3 · authority: `fonttools` · fixture: `cff2-vf`</sub>

### `container.read-woff`

**A WOFF input is read and sliced like the sfnt it wraps**

WOFF is defined as a lossless repackaging of an sfnt: the WOFF 1.0 specification states that the format 'is a simple repackaging of the table-based sfnt structure' and that decoding reproduces the original tables byte for byte. A tool that accepts `.woff` in its open dialog (`dialogs.py:44`) therefore has no excuse for behaving differently on it, and the outlines of a slice from the WOFF must be the same as from the TTF. This is the input half of A3; the output half is tested separately.

<sub>covers A3, H1 · authority: `fonttools` · fixture: `recursive-vf-woff`</sub>

### `container.read-woff2`

**A WOFF2 input is read and sliced like the sfnt it wraps**

WOFF2 applies a reversible transform to `glyf` and `loca` before compressing, so unlike WOFF it does not simply hold the original bytes; the WOFF2 specification requires the transform to be exactly invertible and the reconstructed tables to be equivalent. That makes reading WOFF2 the strongest test that the input decoder is faithful, because a bug in the glyf reconstruction shows up directly as wrong outlines. If the outlines from the WOFF2 input match the source at the same location, the transform was reversed correctly.

<sub>covers A3, H1 · authority: `fonttools` · fixture: `recursive-vf-woff2`</sub>

### `container.ttf-in-otf-out`

**Typing .otf for a TrueType font does not convert the outlines**

`.ttf` and `.otf` name the same container — a bare sfnt — and differ only in convention about which outline format is inside. Converting quadratic `glyf` curves to CFF cubics is a lossy re-drawing of every glyph that the user did not ask for, and the OpenType specification treats the outline format as a property of the font, not of the filename. So the honest reading of H1 is that the extension selects the *container*, and `.ttf` versus `.otf` selects nothing: the output must still be a glyf-flavoured sfnt.

<sub>covers H1 · authority: `judgement` · fixture: `recursive-vf`</sub>

### `container.ttf-in-ttf-out`

**A TrueType input saved with a .ttf name is a bare sfnt**

This is the baseline every other container case is compared against, and the only combination on which the original and the corrected behaviour are certain to agree. `sfnt_flavor` must be `truetype`: an sfnt with sfntVersion 0x00010000 and a `glyf` table, no WOFF wrapper. It also fixes the reference output that the WOFF and WOFF2 round-trip cases assert equality against, so its id is load-bearing and must not be renamed.

<sub>covers A3, H1 · authority: `fonttools` · fixture: `recursive-vf`</sub>

### `container.ttf-in-woff-out`

**Typing .woff for a TrueType input must produce a WOFF**

H1 states the output container follows the extension the user types, and a user who types `.woff` is asking for a web font. **The original fails this case.** `TTFont.save` does not look at the filename at all: it passes `self.flavor` to `SFNTWriter` (`ttFont.py:411`), and `self.flavor` was copied from the reader when the input was opened (`ttFont.py:318`), so a TTF input always writes a bare sfnt no matter what it is called. Verified with fontTools 4.62.1: slicing `Recursive-VF.subset.ttf` to `o.woff` yields a file whose flavor is `None`. Shipping an sfnt named `.woff` is a real defect, because a server sending it as `font/woff` produces a font a browser rejects.

<sub>covers H1 · authority: `slice-ui` · fixture: `recursive-vf`</sub>

### `container.ttf-in-woff2-out`

**Typing .woff2 for a TrueType input must produce a WOFF2**

Same contract as the WOFF case and the same defect in the original: verified with fontTools 4.62.1, saving a TTF-read font to `o.woff2` produces a bare sfnt of exactly the size of the sfnt, with flavor `None`. **The original fails this case.** WOFF2 is where it matters most in practice, since it is the only container most sites actually deploy, and a mislabelled sfnt is unusable there. The check is `sfnt_flavor` = `woff2` together with an outline check, because a container that is right but whose glyf reconstruction is wrong is no better than the wrong container.

<sub>covers H1 · authority: `slice-ui` · fixture: `recursive-vf`</sub>

### `container.woff-in-ttf-out`

**A WOFF input saved with a .ttf name must produce a bare sfnt**

The mirror image of the previous two, and the direction in which the original's behaviour is most surprising. **The original fails this case:** because the flavor is inherited from the reader, a WOFF input always writes a WOFF, so a user who opens a `.woff` and saves as `.ttf` gets a WOFF file with a `.ttf` name — verified with fontTools 4.62.1, flavor `woff`, 1628 bytes. A desktop font manager asked to install that file will reject it. H1 says the extension decides, and the extension here says sfnt.

<sub>covers A3, H1 · authority: `slice-ui` · fixture: `recursive-vf-woff`</sub>

### `container.woff-in-woff-out`

**A WOFF input saved as .woff stays a WOFF**

The one WOFF-output combination the original gets right, and it gets it right by accident: the flavor is inherited from the input rather than chosen from the extension, and here the two happen to agree. Including it makes the failure pattern of the four cross-container cases interpretable — a runner that fails all of `ttf-in-woff-out`, `woff-in-ttf-out` and their WOFF2 twins but passes this one is inheriting the flavor, not ignoring containers entirely. The outline check is carried through so that a WOFF-to-WOFF path is not exempt from G13.

<sub>covers A3, H1 · authority: `fonttools` · fixture: `recursive-vf-woff`</sub>

### `container.woff-input-roundtrips-to-ttf-input`

**Slicing the WOFF fixture gives the same result as slicing the TTF fixture**

`recursive-vf` and `recursive-vf-woff` are the same font in two containers, so the losslessness of WOFF means slicing either with the same settings must give the same font. This is the input-side counterpart of the output round-trip and it catches a different fault: a reader that loses a table WOFF happens to store differently, or that reorders the glyph set. Because both sides go through the identical instancing, the comparison is exact and needs no tolerance.

<sub>covers A3, H1 · authority: `spec` · fixture: `recursive-vf-woff`</sub>

### `container.woff-output-roundtrips-to-ttf-output`

**The same slice written as WOFF holds the same tables and outlines as written as TTF**

WOFF is specified as a lossless container: the WOFF 1.0 specification requires that decoding reproduce the sfnt table data exactly, and that the format add no capability beyond compression and metadata. So two runs of the identical job differing only in the typed extension must yield the same table inventory, the same glyph order and byte-identical outlines once the wrapper is removed. This is a much stronger invariant than checking each output against the source independently, because it admits no rounding slack at all: the two outputs come from the same instanced font.

<sub>covers H1 · authority: `spec` · fixture: `recursive-vf`</sub>

### `container.woff-preserves-hinting`

**Wrapping a hinted font in WOFF does not drop its hinting tables**

WOFF stores whatever tables the sfnt had, with no table-specific knowledge, so `prep`, `fpgm` and `cvt ` must survive the wrapper untouched. The reason to test it explicitly is that hinting tables are the ones an over-eager 'web optimization' step is most tempted to strip, and stripping them changes rendering on every Windows machine using the ClearType v1 path. Slicing is not subsetting, and nothing about choosing a web container authorizes discarding a font's rasterization program.

<sub>covers H1 · authority: `spec` · fixture: `hinted`</sub>

### `container.woff2-in-ttf-out`

**A WOFF2 input saved with a .ttf name must produce a bare sfnt**

**The original fails this case** for the same inherited-flavor reason: a WOFF2 input saved to `o.ttf` comes back with flavor `woff2`, verified with fontTools 4.62.1. Decoding WOFF2 and re-encoding it as WOFF2 also silently re-runs the glyf transform, so this case additionally confirms that a full decode-to-sfnt path exists and is exercised rather than the input bytes being passed through. The outline check is what proves the decode was faithful and not merely a repackaging.

<sub>covers A3, H1 · authority: `slice-ui` · fixture: `recursive-vf-woff2`</sub>

### `container.woff2-in-woff2-out`

**A WOFF2 input saved as .woff2 stays a WOFF2**

The WOFF2 twin of the previous case, and the one that puts the full WOFF2 decode/encode cycle under an outline check: the input transform is reversed on read and re-applied on write, so a bug in either direction moves coordinates. Because the WOFF2 glyf transform is specified as exactly invertible, there is no error budget on the container itself; the 0.5 tolerance here is entirely the instancing rounding allowance, not a container allowance. Any outline error above that is a codec bug, not quantization.

<sub>covers A3, H1 · authority: `fonttools` · fixture: `recursive-vf-woff2`</sub>

### `container.woff2-input-roundtrips-to-ttf-input`

**Slicing the WOFF2 fixture gives the same result as slicing the TTF fixture**

The WOFF2 input path reconstructs `glyf` and `loca` from a transformed representation, so this is the case that proves the reconstruction is exact rather than merely plausible. Comparing against the TTF-input result rather than against the variable source removes the instancing rounding from the comparison entirely, leaving only the codec under test. A WOFF2 decoder that gets composite glyph flags or the overlap-simple bit wrong will show up here and nowhere else in the corpus.

<sub>covers A3, H1 · authority: `spec` · fixture: `recursive-vf-woff2`</sub>

### `container.woff2-output-roundtrips-to-ttf-output`

**The same slice written as WOFF2 holds the same tables and outlines as written as TTF**

WOFF2 compresses harder and transforms `glyf`/`loca`, but the WOFF2 specification still requires the decoded font to be functionally identical to the input sfnt, with the transform exactly reversible. Equality against the TTF output is therefore the right expectation and admits no tolerance: if a coordinate differs by one unit, the transform is not being reversed correctly. This is the check that would catch a WOFF2 encoder that quietly drops a table it thinks is redundant, which byte-size or parse checks would not.

<sub>covers H1 · authority: `spec` · fixture: `recursive-vf`</sub>

### `container.woff2-preserves-glyph-names`

**A WOFF2 round trip keeps the post table's glyph names**

WOFF2 defines an optional transform for the `post` version 2.0 table's name storage, and a decoder that mishandles it silently renames glyphs to `glyph00001` style placeholders. Glyph names are not cosmetic: they are how `GSUB` rules, this corpus's own `contour_count` and `substitutes` checks, and any downstream tooling identify glyphs. This fixture's `post` is format 2.0 with the names `.notdef`, `a` and `a.italic`, so the names surviving is directly observable.

<sub>covers A3, H1 · authority: `spec` · fixture: `recursive-vf-woff2`</sub>

### `container.zopfli-is-not-a-correctness-property`

**WOFF compression strength is deliberately not tested**

H2 records that the original sets `sfnt.USE_ZOPFLI = True` before saving (`instanceworker.py:69`), but zopfli emits an ordinary DEFLATE stream: the WOFF 1.0 specification requires only that each table be compressed with zlib, and a decoder cannot tell which encoder produced the bytes. The only observable difference is file size, and asserting a size would fail any implementation that used a different but equally valid deflate library, which is a test of the toolchain rather than of the font. This case therefore covers H2 by asserting what actually matters — that the WOFF decodes to the right font — and records that no size or encoder assertion belongs in this corpus.

<sub>covers H2 · authority: `judgement` · fixture: `recursive-vf`</sub>

### `outlines.advances-match-source-at-interior`

**Advance widths in a static instance match the source's advances at that location**

An outline that is right with an advance that is wrong still ruins the text: spacing is as much a part of the instance as the shape. Advances at a location come from `hmtx` plus the `HVAR` item variation store, and this fixture has an `HVAR`, so an implementation that applies gvar but forgets HVAR produces correct glyphs at the wrong widths. `hmtx.advanceWidth` is uint16 (OpenType `hmtx`), so half a unit of rounding is again the natural bound; on this fixture fontTools reproduces the reference advances exactly, so 0.5 is generous.

<sub>covers G13 · authority: `fonttools` · fixture: `recursive-vf`</sub>

### `outlines.advances-match-source-at-mono-extreme`

**Advance widths match at the MONO=1 corner, where they change the most**

Recursive's `MONO` axis exists to change advance widths, so MONO=1 is the location where an HVAR mistake produces the largest visible error and the easiest one to diagnose. At a corner every region scalar is 0 or 1, so the reference advance is an exact integer and no rounding allowance is needed. Checking advances at both an interior point and a corner separates 'HVAR ignored entirely' from 'HVAR interpolated wrongly'.

<sub>covers G13 · authority: `fonttools` · fixture: `recursive-vf`</sub>

### `outlines.composites-advances-match`

**Composite glyph advances are not disturbed by instancing**

A composite may take its advance from a component via the USE_MY_METRICS flag (OpenType `glyf`), so an implementation that rebuilds composites, reorders components, or decomposes them can move the advance without touching a single outline coordinate. Advances are exact integers in `hmtx`, and instancing has no reason to change them beyond applying HVAR, so the reference is exact to within the same half-unit rounding as any other advance. Checking this separately from the outline check is what distinguishes 'the shape moved' from 'the shape is right but sits in the wrong box'.

<sub>covers G13 · authority: `fonttools` · fixture: `composites`</sub>

### `outlines.composites-static-matches`

**Composite glyphs instance to the right outlines, including a nested one**

A composite's shape depends on its components' outlines *and* on its own component offsets, both of which vary, so it is the one glyph kind where two independent delta paths must agree. Nesting two deep means a rounding error in the inner composite's offset is inherited by the outer one, so the error budget compounds: each level rounds its offset to int16 (OpenType `glyf`, composite glyph description, ARG_1_AND_2_ARE_WORDS), and a scaled component multiplies its base glyph's own rounding. That is why this case uses the check's default tolerance of 1.0 rather than the 0.5 used for simple contours: half a unit per level, two levels.

<sub>covers G13 · authority: `fonttools` · fixture: `composites`</sub>

### `outlines.contour-structure-preserved`

**Instancing does not change how many contours a glyph has**

Variation deltas move points; they cannot add, remove or merge contours, because gvar deltas are indexed by point number against a fixed point set (OpenType `gvar`, 'the number of deltas must match the number of points in the glyph'). So a static instance must have exactly the contour and point structure of the source glyph. `a` in this fixture has two contours, an outer and a counter, and an instance that reports any other number has rebuilt the glyph rather than interpolated it.

<sub>covers G13 · authority: `spec` · fixture: `recursive-vf`</sub>

### `outlines.hinted-static-matches`

**Instancing a hinted font does not move its outlines**

Hinting is a program that runs at rasterization time and never alters the stored coordinates, so the presence of `prep`, `fpgm`, `cvt ` and glyph instructions must make no difference at all to the outlines an instance carries. An implementation that decompiles and recompiles glyphs in order to preserve or strip instructions is exactly the kind that perturbs coordinates in passing, and this case catches that. Tolerance is 0.5, unchanged from the unhinted case, because nothing about hinting justifies a larger error budget.

<sub>covers G13 · authority: `fonttools` · fixture: `hinted`</sub>

### `outlines.partial-instance-matches-across`

**A partially instanced font still interpolates correctly across the surviving axis**

When some axes are pinned and one is left, the output is still variable and G13 has to hold at every location in the reduced space, not just at its default. This is strictly harder than the static case: the gvar tuples for the pinned axes must be folded into the base outlines and into the surviving axis's deltas, and an implementation that gets the default right can still get the ends of the surviving axis wrong. Sampling the retained range at its minimum, middle and maximum catches exactly that failure. The tolerance is 0.5 for the same int16 reason, applied to the interpolated result at each sample.

<sub>covers G2, G13 · authority: `fonttools` · fixture: `recursive-vf`</sub>

### `outlines.static-matches-source-at-default`

**A static instance pinned at every axis default has the variable font's default outlines**

The default location is the one place where no interpolation happens at all: the glyf table already holds those coordinates and every gvar delta scales to zero, so the instance must reproduce them exactly. Any deviation here is not rounding, it is a bug in delta application or in the normalization of the requested location onto the axis. This is the cheapest possible check of G13 and the one whose failure localizes the fault fastest, which is why it is worth having separately from the interior-location cases.

<sub>covers G13 · authority: `fonttools` · fixture: `recursive-vf`</sub>

### `outlines.static-matches-source-at-extremes`

**A static instance pinned at the axis extremes matches the source rendered there**

At a corner of the design space every axis normalizes to exactly +/-1, so each region's scalar is 1 or 0 and the deltas are applied undivided; the arithmetic is exact and the result must be integer-identical to the source. Corners are also where a sign error or a swapped peak/intermediate tuple shows up most loudly, because that is where the deltas are largest. A tolerance of zero is therefore defensible here and is deliberately stricter than the interior case.

<sub>covers G13 · authority: `fonttools` · fixture: `recursive-vf`</sub>

### `outlines.static-matches-source-at-fractional`

**A pin at a fractional user coordinate matches the source rendered there**

A user coordinate that is not a round number exercises the full chain: `float()` parsing, normalization to F2Dot14, the `avar` segment map, region scalars, and one final rounding to int16. Locations like wght=653.7 are exactly where an implementation that normalizes with the wrong precision, or that rounds the normalized coordinate to F2Dot14 at the wrong moment, drifts away from the reference. Half a unit is still the right bound, for the same int16 reason as the interior case, and it holds empirically on this fixture at this location.

<sub>covers G13 · authority: `fonttools` · fixture: `recursive-vf`</sub>

### `outlines.static-matches-source-at-interior`

**A static instance pinned inside the design space matches the source rendered there**

G13 is the whole point of instancing: the sliced font must draw what a variation-aware renderer draws for the source at the same location, or the slice has silently changed the design. The tolerance is half a unit because glyf coordinates are int16 (OpenType `glyf`, simple glyph description), so a renderer's floating-point interpolated position must be rounded exactly once to reach the static instance and can differ by no more than 0.5 units. Measured against fontTools 4.62.1 on this fixture the largest disagreement over all glyphs at wght=650 and other interior locations is 0.4998 units, so 0.5 is tight but achievable; anything above it is a real disagreement about the shape, not quantization.

<sub>covers G13 · authority: `fonttools` · fixture: `recursive-vf`</sub>

### `outlines.two-axis-partial-matches-across`

**Pinning one of two axes leaves the other interpolating correctly**

Folding a pinned axis into a two-dimensional delta set is the smallest case in which intermediate-region tuples have to be re-tented onto a lower-dimensional space, and it is where an off-by-one in region indexing shows up without any avar or feature-variation noise. If the surviving axis interpolates correctly at its minimum, default and maximum after the fold, the reduction preserved the design; if it is right only at the default, the deltas were dropped rather than folded. The tolerance is 0.5, the int16 quantization bound.

<sub>covers G2, G13 · authority: `fonttools` · fixture: `two-axis`</sub>

### `outlines.two-axis-static-matches`

**A minimal two-axis font instances to the right outlines**

`recursive-vf` has an `avar`, feature variations and five axes, so a failure there has many possible causes; `two-axis` is the control, with simple contours, two axes and nothing else, so a failure can only be delta application. Having the same property tested on both a minimal and a realistic fixture is what makes a G13 failure diagnosable rather than merely visible. The fixture is specified to carry `wght` 100-900 default 400 and `wdth` 75-125 default 100, and this case pins an interior point on both.

<sub>covers G13 · authority: `fonttools` · fixture: `two-axis`</sub>

### `overlap.advances-are-not-changed`

**Overlap removal does not change any advance width**

Overlap removal is an operation on outlines; advance width is metrics, and nothing about merging two contours tells you anything about how much room the glyph should occupy. fontTools is explicit about the boundary: after replacing a glyph it rewrites only the left side bearing to match the new `xMin`, leaving the width alone — `hmtxTable[glyphName] = (width, glyph.xMin)` (`ttLib/removeOverlaps.py`). An implementation that recomputes advances from the merged bounding box would reflow every line of text set in the font. **The original never removes overlaps** (G14) and is expected to fail.

<sub>covers G14 · authority: `fonttools` · fixture: `overlapping` · **the original does not have this feature**</sub>

### `overlap.clean-glyph-is-left-alone`

**A glyph with no overlaps is not rebuilt**

Passing a clean glyph through a boolean engine costs something and gains nothing: the engine renumbers points, may re-fit curves through rounded intersection points that were never needed, and can convert an exact quadratic into an approximation. fontTools takes exactly this position -- `removeTTGlyphOverlaps` compares the simplified path with the original and replaces the glyph only `if not _same_path(path, path2)` (`ttLib/removeOverlaps.py`). So `clean` must come out of a removal run with the same points, in the same order, as the same job produces with the feature off. The comparison is against that control run rather than against the source font, because instancing to wght=400 moves every outline on its own, and it is scoped to `clean` because `bars` in the same font is required to change -- `overlap.two-bars-merge-into-one-contour` asserts exactly that. Point-level rather than drawn-outline equality is the point: a rebuilt glyph can draw the same shape with different points, and that is the cost this case exists to forbid. **The original never removes overlaps** (G14) and is expected to fail.

<sub>covers G14 · authority: `judgement` · fixture: `overlapping` · **the original does not have this feature**</sub>

### `overlap.control-same-job-without-removal`

**The same slice with overlap removal off, as a control for what removal changes**

Not an obligation of its own but the baseline the removal cases measure against. It runs exactly the job `overlap.clean-glyph-is-left-alone` runs, with the one checkbox off, so that any difference between the two outputs is attributable to overlap removal and nothing else. Comparing a removal run against the *source* font cannot do that job, because instancing to wght=400 changes the outlines by itself. Every implementation is expected to pass this, including the original, which is simply doing an ordinary slice.

<sub>covers G14 · authority: `judgement` · fixture: `overlapping`</sub>

### `overlap.counter-inside-a-counter-survives`

**A circled letter keeps all four levels of its nesting**

A circled 'o' nests fill inside hole inside fill inside hole: ring outer, ring counter, letter outer, letter counter. This is the case that rules out the naive algorithm of unioning the outward-wound contours and subtracting the inward-wound ones, which is correct only to depth two and turns the letter inside the ring into a hole at depth three. The non-zero winding rule counts crossings rather than alternating, so the right implementation is winding-aware at arbitrary depth. **The original never removes overlaps** (G14) and is expected to fail; a naive new implementation is expected to fail here while passing the plain-counter case, which is exactly why both exist.

<sub>covers G14 · authority: `spec` · fixture: `overlapping` · **the original does not have this feature**</sub>

### `overlap.counter-survives`

**The counter of an 'o' is still a hole after overlap removal**

TrueType fills with the non-zero winding rule (OpenType `glyf`), under which a counter is a contour wound opposite to the outer contour and therefore subtracts. A boolean-union implementation that treats every contour as an additive region fills counters in and destroys 'o', 'e', 'a', 'B' and 'p' throughout the font — a failure that is invisible to any outline-coordinate comparison but obvious to `filled_region_matches`. Two contours must remain and the hole must remain a hole. **The original never removes overlaps** (G14) and is expected to fail.

<sub>covers G14 · authority: `spec` · fixture: `overlapping` · **the original does not have this feature**</sub>

### `overlap.filled-region-preserved-font-wide`

**Overlap removal changes no glyph's filled region anywhere in the font**

This is the defining property of the feature and the reason `filled_region_matches` exists: the outline is *supposed* to change, so comparing coordinates would reject every correct implementation, while comparing the set of points inside the glyph accepts exactly the correct ones. The tolerance is one unit because the merged boundary passes through intersection points computed in floating point and then rounded to the integer grid, so the boundary can move by up to half a unit at a vertex and slightly more where a curve is refitted through rounded points. Anything beyond a unit is a change of shape, not of representation. **The original never removes overlaps** (G14) and is expected to fail.

<sub>covers G14 · authority: `judgement` · fixture: `overlapping` · **the original does not have this feature**</sub>

### `overlap.fixture-actually-overlaps`

**Without overlap removal the overlapping fixture really does self-intersect**

Every case in this section asserts that overlaps are gone, and all of them would pass vacuously against a fixture that never had any. This case is the control: with `remove_overlaps` off, `no_self_intersections` must *fail*, which is asserted here with `not`. It also records the pre-removal state that the untouched-glyph and advance-preservation cases compare against, so its id is load-bearing.

<sub>covers G12, G14 · authority: `fonttools` · fixture: `overlapping`</sub>

### `overlap.hinting-is-dropped`

**Removing overlaps drops the font's hinting**

TrueType instructions address points by index (`SRP0`, `MDAP`, `IUP` and the rest all take point numbers), and the CVT program's assumptions about which point is which stop holding the moment contours are merged and points renumbered. Running a stale program against a new point set does not degrade gracefully; it moves the wrong points and distorts the glyph at small sizes. fontTools takes the same view and drops hinting from the whole font by default, noting that 'removing overlaps invalidates the hinting' and that leaving only some glyphs hinted 'would look weird' (`ttLib/removeOverlaps.py`). **The original never removes overlaps** (G14) and is expected to fail.

<sub>covers G14 · authority: `judgement` · fixture: `hinted` · **the original does not have this feature**</sub>

### `overlap.hinting-kept-when-not-removing`

**Instancing alone does not drop hinting**

The previous case's justification for dropping hinting is specific to renumbered points, so it must not leak into the ordinary path: instancing moves points but does not add, remove or reorder them, so instructions remain valid and must be kept. Without this case an implementation could 'pass' the hinting-dropped case by never shipping hinting at all, which would silently degrade every font the tool touches. Together the two cases say precisely when hinting may be discarded and when it may not.

<sub>covers G13, G14 · authority: `fonttools` · fixture: `hinted`</sub>

### `overlap.metrics-tables-recalculated`

**head and maxp describe the merged outlines, not the originals**

Merging contours changes point counts and can change the bounding box, and both are recorded in tables that renderers trust without re-deriving: `head.xMin`/`yMin`/`xMax`/`yMax` and `maxp.maxPoints`/`maxContours` (OpenType `head`, `maxp`). A rasterizer that allocates a point buffer from `maxp.maxPoints` will overflow or truncate if the value is stale. So the recalculation G8 already requires on save has to happen *after* removal, not before it. **The original never removes overlaps** (G14) and is expected to fail this case.

<sub>covers G8, G14 · authority: `spec` · fixture: `overlapping` · **the original does not have this feature**</sub>

### `overlap.no-overlap-flags-after-removal`

**A font with overlaps removed does not claim to have overlaps**

`OVERLAP_SIMPLE` and `OVERLAP_COMPOUND` tell a rasterizer 'this glyph self-overlaps, composite it before filling' (OpenType `glyf`, simple glyph flags), which on some rasterizers is a slower path and on others changes anti-aliasing at the seams. Setting them on a font whose overlaps have just been removed is a false statement about the outlines and gives up the performance the removal was for. fontTools treats the two as mutually exclusive branches of the same `if`, setting flags only under `KEEP_AND_SET_FLAGS` and never under `REMOVE` (`varLib/instancer/__init__.py`). **The original never removes overlaps** (G14): it always takes the flag-setting branch (G12) and is expected to fail.

<sub>covers G12, G14 · authority: `spec` · fixture: `overlapping` · **the original does not have this feature**</sub>

### `overlap.no-self-intersections-font-wide`

**No glyph in the output has a contour crossing itself or another**

The point of the feature is to produce outlines usable by consumers that cannot handle overlaps — PostScript printers, the CFF outline format, and pre-composition renderers that stroke rather than fill. A per-glyph pass that resolves the glyphs the test happens to name but leaves others intersecting delivers none of that, so the property has to be asserted over the whole font. Paired with the control case, which asserts the same font *does* self-intersect before removal, this is a real before/after and not a tautology. **The original never removes overlaps** (G14) and is expected to fail.

<sub>covers G14 · authority: `judgement` · fixture: `overlapping` · **the original does not have this feature**</sub>

### `overlap.non-overlapping-composite-is-not-decomposed`

**A composite whose components do not overlap keeps its components**

Composites exist to share outline data; decomposing them for no reason multiplies a font's `glyf` size by the number of times each base glyph is reused, which for an accented Latin font is substantial. Since there is no overlap to resolve, decomposing buys nothing and costs both size and the USE_MY_METRICS relationship between the composite and its base. fontTools decomposes only when `componentsOverlap` returns true, and that restraint is the correct behaviour, not an implementation detail. **The original never removes overlaps** (G14) and is expected to fail.

<sub>covers G14 · authority: `judgement` · fixture: `composites` · **the original does not have this feature**</sub>

### `overlap.output-in-woff2-is-still-clean`

**Overlap removal and a WOFF2 container compose without interfering**

The WOFF2 glyf transform re-encodes point flags and coordinates, and removal has just rewritten every merged glyph's point set, so this pairing is where an ordering bug — transforming before merging, or recomputing `loca` from stale data — would surface. There is no reason the two features should interact, and asserting that they do not is cheaper than debugging it later. The filled region and the absence of self-intersections must both survive the round trip through the container. **The original never removes overlaps** (G14) and is expected to fail.

<sub>covers G14, H1 · authority: `judgement` · fixture: `overlapping` · **the original does not have this feature**</sub>

### `overlap.overlapping-components-are-merged`

**A composite whose components overlap is decomposed and merged**

A composite's overlap lives between its components, not inside any one of them, so it cannot be resolved without flattening the glyph into contours first; fontTools decomposes exactly and only in that case, testing `componentsOverlap` before replacing the glyph (`ttLib/removeOverlaps.py`). The result must be a simple glyph, because a composite by definition re-instantiates its base glyphs and cannot express the merged boundary. The filled region is again the invariant: decomposition plus merge changes the description completely while the picture stays put. **The original never removes overlaps** (G14) and is expected to fail.

<sub>covers G14 · authority: `judgement` · fixture: `composites` · **the original does not have this feature**</sub>

### `overlap.removal-does-not-change-glyph-count`

**Overlap removal neither adds nor removes glyphs**

Glyph IDs are the currency of `cmap`, `GSUB`, `GPOS` and `hmtx`; inserting or dropping a glyph renumbers all of them and breaks every reference in the font. Decomposing a composite is a change to one glyph's description, not to the glyph inventory, so the count must be unchanged even where composites are flattened. This is the invariant that catches an implementation that, say, appends merged results as new glyphs rather than replacing them in place. **The original never removes overlaps** (G14) and is expected to fail.

<sub>covers G14 · authority: `spec` · fixture: `overlapping` · **the original does not have this feature**</sub>

### `overlap.requires-a-static-font`

**Overlap removal on a still-variable output must be refused, not ignored**

`gvar` deltas are addressed by point number against a fixed point set (OpenType `gvar`: the delta count must match the glyph's point count), and merging contours renumbers and re-counts the points, so every delta in the font would then refer to a different point. There is no way to remove overlaps from a font that is still variable and keep it correct; fontTools agrees and simply skips the work, guarding it with `if 'fvar' not in varfont` and documenting that 'the overlap parameter only has effect when generating full static instances' (`varLib/instancer/__init__.py`). Silently doing nothing when the user ticked the box is the same defect shape as B8, whose adjudicated verdict in this project is that an unsupported request must be refused rather than quietly reinterpreted, so the correct behaviour is a clear error. **The original has no such option at all** (G14) and fails this case for a different reason.

<sub>covers G14, G2 · authority: `judgement` · fixture: `recursive-vf` · **the original does not have this feature** · expects a refusal mentioning `overlap`, `static`</sub>

### `overlap.self-intersecting-contour-resolved`

**A contour that crosses itself is resolved without changing the filled region**

A single contour that crosses itself — a figure-eight or a bowtie — has no 'other contour' to union with, so an implementation built only around pairwise contour booleans has nothing to do and leaves it alone. Under non-zero winding a bowtie fills both lobes and a figure-eight cancels its inner region, so the correct result depends on the crossing's orientation and cannot be guessed. Requiring `no_self_intersections` on the output while requiring the filled region to be unchanged pins down both halves of the answer. **The original never removes overlaps** (G14) and is expected to fail.

<sub>covers G14 · authority: `judgement` · fixture: `overlapping` · **the original does not have this feature**</sub>

### `overlap.two-bars-merge-into-one-contour`

**Two crossing bars become a single contour with the same filled region**

Two crossing rectangles under the non-zero winding rule fill a plus sign; removing the overlap must produce the outline of that plus sign, which is one contour of twelve points, not two rectangles. This is the simplest possible statement of what overlap removal means, and the contour count is the observable that distinguishes 'merged' from 'left alone but flagged'. The filled region must be identical because the rendered result was already the plus sign — overlap removal changes the description, never the picture. **The original never removes overlaps** (G14): it passes no `overlap` argument to `instantiateVariableFont`, so it is expected to fail this case.

<sub>covers G14 · authority: `judgement` · fixture: `overlapping` · **the original does not have this feature**</sub>

## partial-instancing

Narrowing the design space while the font stays variable — fewer axes, or the same axes over smaller ranges. Harder than pinning, because the variation data has to be rewritten to say the same thing about a smaller space rather than simply discarded.

Covers claims: B1, B2, B3, B5, B6, B7, B9, C1, G1, G10, G13, G2, G3, G4, G5, G6, G8.

### `partial.advances-still-vary-across-a-restricted-range`

**Advance widths still vary across a narrowed axis, not frozen at the default**

A variable font's `hmtx` holds only the default master's advances; the variation lives in `HVAR`, or for a `glyf` font in the phantom points `gvar` carries at the end of every glyph. An implementation that narrows an axis and drops one of those without rescaling the other produces a font that still looks right at its default location and has frozen widths everywhere else -- text set at any other weight or width then mis-spaces, with outlines that are perfectly correct. Nothing else in the corpus can see that: every other advance check samples a single location, and a frozen font passes at whichever location happens to be its default. `two-axis` is the fixture because its masters really do differ in advance -- `H` runs 372 at wdth=50, 600 at 100 and 960 at 200 -- so the three samples here separate a font whose widths still interpolate from one whose widths are constant.

<sub>covers G2, G13 · authority: `fonttools` · fixture: `two-axis`</sub>

### `partial.avar-renormalized-across-restricted-range`

**avar is renormalized onto the narrowed extent, so weights still land where they did**

After restricting wght to 300:700, the value 700 normalizes to +1 where it used to normalize to about +0.571; if avar's map were carried over unchanged, every weight in the surviving range would be evaluated at the wrong point of the segment map and the outlines would be wrong everywhere except the default. G3 says fontTools rewrites the map, and measurement confirms it: the wght map becomes {-1: -1, 0: 0, 0.25006103515625: 0.48614501953125, 0.5: 0.657470703125, 0.75006103515625: 0.8287353515625, 1: 1}. The observable consequence — and the reason this is checked with outlines rather than table contents — is that the sliced font drawn at wght 550 must match the source drawn at wght 550; measured maximum coordinate deviation across 300, 350, 400, 550 and 700 was 0.5 units, comfortably inside the tolerance.

### `partial.avar-survives-with-its-axis`

**avar is kept when an axis that has a segment map survives**

avar's segment maps are what make Recursive's wght axis perceptually even; dropping the table would silently change every interpolated weight, because the normalized coordinate a renderer computes from fvar would no longer be corrected. A partial slice that keeps wght must therefore keep wght's map. Measured: the output still has an avar, carrying the wght map alone once the other four axes are pinned — the pinned axes' maps go with their axes, because avar maps are positional against fvar's axis order.

<sub>covers G2, G3 · authority: `fonttools` · fixture: `recursive-vf`</sub>

### `partial.axis-order-preserved-first-and-last`

**Surviving axes keep their original fvar order (MONO, CRSV)**

The companion to the previous case, chosen so that the two survivors are the first and last of the five, with three removed from between them. If a program rebuilt fvar by iterating the user's edits rather than the font's axis list, this is the case that would come out as CRSV, MONO — and every positional reference into fvar would then point at the wrong axis. Measured: fontTools yields MONO then CRSV.

<sub>covers C1, G2 · authority: `fonttools` · fixture: `recursive-vf`</sub>

### `partial.axis-order-preserved-first-and-third`

**Surviving axes keep their original fvar order (MONO, wght)**

fvar's axis order is not cosmetic: it is the index space that avar segment maps, gvar tuple regions, item variation store regions, named-instance coordinate arrays and GSUB/GPOS condition tables all address axes by. Removing axes must therefore compact the list in place rather than reorder it, and the surviving axes must appear in the order the source font declared them. Recursive-VF declares MONO, CASL, wght, slnt, CRSV; pinning CASL, slnt and CRSV must leave MONO before wght, which is what fontTools produces.

<sub>covers C1, G2 · authority: `fonttools` · fixture: `recursive-vf`</sub>

### `partial.axis-order-preserved-restricted-plus-whole`

**Order holds when one survivor is restricted and the other is left whole**

B1 says an empty cell leaves an axis alone, and B2 says a cell with a colon restricts it; the two kinds of survivor must end up in the same list, ordered by the source fvar and not by which kind they are. wght is Recursive's third axis and CRSV its fifth, so a correct output declares wght first even though CRSV was the axis the user did not touch. Measured: wght 300/300/700 then CRSV 0/0.5/1.

<sub>covers B1, B2, C1, G2 · authority: `fonttools` · fixture: `recursive-vf`</sub>

### `partial.centred-default-asymmetric-restriction`

**Trimming only the upper half leaves the lower half's mapping alone**

100:650 leaves the lower half of the centred axis exactly as it was and shrinks only the upper half, so the two halves must be rescaled by different factors — 1 and 500/250. This is the sharpest test of independent renormalization: a program using one span for the whole axis would either distort the untouched half or leave the trimmed half unscaled, and either error is invisible at the default. Sampling below, at and above the default is what makes both failures observable.

<sub>covers B7, G2, G13 · authority: `fonttools` · fixture: `centred-default`</sub>

### `partial.centred-default-lower-half-only`

**A centred axis trimmed to its default upward stays variable downward**

100:400 keeps the default at the range maximum, which B7 admits, and leaves an axis that varies only below its default. The positive normalized half is then empty, so every gvar tuple whose peak is positive on this axis becomes unreachable and must be dropped while the negative-side deltas are preserved untouched. Getting this wrong shows up as the light end of the axis losing its variation or as leftover deltas that can never fire.

<sub>covers B7, G2, G13 · authority: `fonttools` · fixture: `centred-default`</sub>

### `partial.centred-default-range-above-default-refused`

**On a centred axis, a range above the default is refused**

The `centred-default` fixture runs 100/400/900, so 500:900 asks for the upper part of the axis with the default left outside it. Level 3 cannot move a default, so this must be refused even though the request is a perfectly sensible thing to want — 'give me only the bold half' is a Level 4 operation. The fixture matters because a centred default is where an implementation that only ever tested min-default axes would be most likely to let this through.

<sub>covers B7 · authority: `slice-ui` · fixture: `centred-default` · expects a refusal mentioning `wght`, `default`, `400`</sub>

### `partial.centred-default-symmetric-restriction`

**A centred default keeps its position when both halves are trimmed**

Normalization treats the two sides of a default independently: on a 100/400/900 axis, 250 is halfway down and normalizes to -0.5 while 650 is halfway up and normalizes to +0.5, even though 150 user units separate the first pair and 250 the second. Restricting to 250:650 rescales each half by a different factor — the lower by 300/150 and the upper by 500/250 — so a program that normalizes with a single span would be right at the default and wrong everywhere else. Verified with fontTools on a purpose-built 100/400/900 font: fvar comes out 250/400/650 and the sliced outlines match the source at 250, 300, 400, 500 and 650 to within 0.01 units.

### `partial.centred-default-upper-half-only`

**A centred axis trimmed to its default downward stays variable upward**

The mirror of the previous case: 400:900 keeps the default at the range minimum and leaves only the upper half. Together the two cases show that neither half is privileged — an implementation that special-cased 'default equals minimum' as the only degenerate shape, which is what Recursive's wght would teach it, would fail one of them. The outlines are sampled at both ends and the midpoint so that a collapsed or unscaled half cannot pass.
