### `partial.composites-survive-a-restricted-range`

**Composite glyphs interpolate correctly across a restricted range**

A composite glyph's gvar deltas move its component offsets rather than its points, and a nested composite resolves through two levels of that. Rescaling those deltas onto a narrowed axis is the same arithmetic as for simple contours but a different code path, and an implementation can easily get one right and the other wrong -- the error appears only where components are placed, so a check on the base glyphs alone would miss it. The outlines are compared after component resolution, which is what a renderer sees, at both ends of the restricted range and in the middle, because a mis-scaled delta can still be correct at one endpoint. `composites` carries a single wght axis running 400/400/900, so 400:700 is the narrowing available on it; the axis must survive with gvar intact, since pinning it would test a different code path entirely.

<sub>covers G2, G13 · authority: `fonttools` · fixture: `composites`</sub>

### `partial.default-at-top-of-restricted-range`

**A range whose maximum is the axis default is accepted (the inclusive boundary)**

B7 requires the restricted range to contain the default; containment is inclusive at both ends, and the original's own test is `default < min or default > max`, so a default sitting exactly on the range maximum passes. This is the positive counterpart to the B7 refusals: without it an implementation could satisfy B7 by rejecting every range that does not start at the default. The result is an axis that varies only downward from its default, perfectly expressible in fvar since minValue, defaultValue and maxValue are three independent Fixed values with only min <= default <= max required. Measured with fontTools: CRSV comes out as 0/0.5/0.5 and the font is still variable.

### `partial.degenerate-range-is-a-pin`

**A range of zero width behaves as a pin and removes the axis**

`0:0` parses as a range under B2 and passes B7 because slnt's default is 0, but a range containing exactly one location is not a design space — there is nothing left to interpolate. An fvar record with min = default = max would advertise an axis a renderer can do nothing with, so collapsing it to a pin is the only coherent outcome. Measured: with the other four axes pinned as well, fontTools removes fvar entirely and the output is static, which is the correct reading and worth pinning down because a naive implementation would instead emit a zero-width axis.

### `partial.featurevars-all-records-die-but-axes-survive`

**When every condition dies, no substitution is left behind**

MONO and wght both survive here, and MONO is one of the axes the source conditions test, but CRSV is pinned to its default so no record can fire. The requirement is that nothing conditional remains active and no condition indexes a missing axis. This case deliberately does not assert `no_feature_variations`: fontTools 4.62.1 leaves an empty FeatureVariations table behind in exactly this shape — zero records, still written to the file — where it removes the table outright when no conditioned axis survives. That is harmless and spec-legal, so failing the case over it would be scoring a wart rather than a defect; `feature_variation_count` is proposed above so the corpus can state `equals: 0` explicitly.

**Restricting the axis below a condition's threshold removes the condition**

Restricting CRSV to 0:0.75 makes that unreachable, so the record must go for the same reason as the pinned-to-default case: it can never fire, and it indexes an axis whose range no longer contains its trigger. This is the range counterpart to partial.featurevars-unreachable-condition-dropped and shows that reachability is judged against the new extents rather than against the new default alone. ### `partial.featurevars-condition-renormalized-to-restricted-range`

**A surviving condition's threshold is renormalized onto the narrowed axis**

Recursive's cursive condition fires at normalized 0.79998779296875, which on the full CRSV axis is design 0.9; restricting CRSV to 0:0.95 rescales the upper half so that same design value 0.9 now normalizes to about 0.8888512138885122, and fontTools rewrites the condition to that. ### `partial.featurevars-folded-into-feature-list`

**A condition set that holds at the new default is folded into the feature itself**

### `partial.fvar-narrowed-extent`

**A restricted range narrows the surviving axis's fvar extent**

### `partial.no-avar-fixture-does-not-gain-one`

A font with no avar has the identity mapping by definition, and the identity resampled onto any sub-range is still the identity, so there is nothing to record; emitting an avar full of identity segments would add bytes and a new opportunity for rounding error for no benefit. ### `partial.output-is-a-well-formed-variable-font`

**A partial slice is a font a renderer can load and vary**

Everything else in this file checks one field at a time; this case checks that the whole is a font. A variable TrueType font needs fvar and, to vary its outlines, gvar, and the OpenType specification requires head's bounding box, maxp's maxima and hhea's extremes to describe the glyf data actually present. A partial slice rewrites glyf and gvar together, so these summary tables have to be recomputed from the result rather than carried over from the source.

### `partial.pinned-off-default-keeps-variable-kerning`

**Kerning stays right when one axis is pinned off its default and another is narrowed**

A `GDEF` item variation store re-tents cleanly as long as every other axis stays at its default, because deltas are measured from the default master and the residual at the new default location is then zero. Pinning an axis *away* from its default breaks that: the kerning at `wdth=50` differs from the kerning at `wdth=100` by exactly that residual, and it has to be written back into the GPOS value records and anchors that address the store. This case existed first as a recorded gap -- the implementation refused the job while fontTools did it -- and the interior sample is what holds the fix honest: a store re-tented without its residual is still exactly right at the default and wrong everywhere else, which no single-location check would notice.

### `partial.range-above-default-refused`

**A restricted range entirely above the axis default is refused**

Level 3 sub-spacing can narrow an axis but cannot move where its default sits, because the default location is the one the glyf outlines themselves encode; every gvar delta is measured from it. Asking for wght 400:700 on an axis whose default is 300 would require rebuilding the default instance at 400, which is Level 4 work the compiler does not do. Refusing is therefore the honest answer, and the message must name the axis and the default so the user can see what to type instead.

Refusing is correct because the user asked for a design space the font cannot provide.

<sub>covers B7, B9 · authority: `slice-ui` · fixture: `recursive-vf` · expects a refusal mentioning `wght`, `default`, `300`</sub>

### `partial.range-equal-to-full-extent-is-a-no-op`

**A range identical to the axis's own extent changes nothing**

Asking for 300:1000 on an axis that already runs 300 to 1000 is a request the tool must accept — B13 only refuses a job in which every cell is empty, and this cell is not — but it removes nothing from the design space, so nothing may be lost. This is the control case for the whole area: it separates 'the program restricts correctly' from 'the program damages the font whenever it touches it'. Measured: all five axes survive with their original extents, all 64 named instances survive, and avar is still present.

<sub>covers B1, B2, G2, G3, G4 · authority: `fonttools` · fixture: `recursive-vf`</sub>

### `partial.range-missing-default-on-centred-axis-refused`

**The rule applies to an axis whose default is in the middle**

CRSV runs 0 to 1 with its default at 0.5, so both 0.6:1 and 0:0.4 exclude the default while sitting entirely inside the axis's own extent — no clamping is involved and the request looks superficially reasonable. It is still refused, for the same reason: a Level 3 slice cannot relocate the default, and moving CRSV's default from 0.5 to 0.6 would mean recomputing every glyph's default outline. The message must name CRSV and its default so the refusal is actionable.

<sub>covers B7 · authority: `slice-ui` · fixture: `recursive-vf` · expects a refusal mentioning `crsv`, `default`, `0.5`</sub>

### `partial.range-with-default-at-its-minimum-accepted`

**A range whose minimum is the default is accepted**

Containment is inclusive, so a default sitting exactly on the range minimum satisfies the Level 3 rule — the default location is inside the requested space and does not have to move. This is the common case for Recursive, whose wght default of 300 is also its minimum, and refusing it would make the axis unrestrictable at all. The positive case is needed alongside the refusals so that an implementation cannot pass B7 by rejecting every range.

<sub>covers B7, G2 · authority: `slice-ui` · fixture: `recursive-vf`</sub>

### `partial.reversed-range-equals-sorted-range`

**700:300 slices the same design space as 300:700**

B6 records that the range parser sorts its two bounds, so the order they were typed in carries no meaning. That is the defensible reading: a range is a set, and the OpenType axis record has a minValue and a maxValue rather than a first and a second. The expectation here is byte-for-byte the same design space as partial.fvar-narrowed-extent, which is the point — the two inputs must not be distinguishable in the output.

<sub>covers B6, B2, G2 · authority: `slice-ui` · fixture: `recursive-vf`</sub>

### `partial.reversed-range-still-checked-against-default`

**A reversed range is sorted first and then checked for the default**

B6 sorts the bounds and B7 then tests containment, so the two rules have to compose: 700:400 becomes 400:700, which still excludes wght's default of 300 and is still refused. Checking containment before sorting would compare 300 against a range whose minimum is 700 and maximum is 400 and could reach either verdict by accident. The order of the two rules is therefore load-bearing and this case pins it.

<sub>covers B6, B7 · authority: `slice-ui` · fixture: `recursive-vf` · expects a refusal mentioning `wght`, `default`, `300`</sub>

### `partial.stat-format4-value-dropped-when-unreachable`

**A format 4 STAT value survives only if every axis it names is still reachable at that point**

Recursive's 'Upright' and 'Italic' are format 4 records, each naming a combination — Upright is slnt 0 with CRSV 0.5, Italic is slnt -15 with CRSV 1. A format 4 record is an all-or-nothing conjunction, so it survives only when every one of its AxisValueRecords is still reachable. Measured: pinning slnt to 0 and CRSV to 0.5 keeps Upright (name ID 413) and drops Italic (414); pinning CRSV to 1 with slnt still at 0 drops both, since neither combination is satisfiable — which is the case checked here.

<sub>covers G5, G10 · authority: `fonttools` · fixture: `recursive-vf`</sub>

### `partial.stat-format4-value-kept-when-reachable`

**The format 4 value the pin actually selects is kept**

The other side of the previous case, so that its expectation cannot be satisfied by a program that simply deletes all format 4 records. Pinning slnt to 0 and CRSV to 0.5 lands exactly on the Upright combination, which remains true of every location the sliced font can render, so it must survive; Italic, which requires slnt -15, cannot. Measured: name ID 413 present, 414 absent.

<sub>covers G5, G10 · authority: `fonttools` · fixture: `recursive-vf`</sub>

### `partial.stat-keeps-records-for-pinned-axes`

**STAT keeps a design axis record for axes the slice removed**

This is the claim in G5 worth confirming rather than assuming, and fontTools 4.62.1 does confirm it: slicing Recursive-VF down to wght alone leaves all five STAT design axis records — MONO, CASL, wght, slnt, CRSV — with AxisOrdering 0 to 4 unchanged. It is the right answer, because the sliced font is still a member of the Recursive family and STAT's job is to say where in that family it sits: a Sans Linear Upright slice is distinguished from its Mono and Casual siblings precisely by the axes it no longer varies on. The observable consequence is that the axis name records 269 to 273 all survive even though only 271 is referenced from fvar, so this case reads them as the proxy for the STAT records that point at them; a direct `stat_design_axis_tags` check is proposed above.

<sub>covers G5, G10 · authority: `fonttools` · fixture: `recursive-vf`</sub>

### `partial.stat-survives-partial-instancing`

**STAT is kept when the output is still variable**

STAT is what lets an operating system place the font inside its family, and the OpenType specification makes it required for variable fonts. A slice that is still variable is still a family member, so removing STAT would leave a conformance hole that no other table fills. G5 says fontTools keeps it, and measurement confirms the table is present in every partial output tried.

<sub>covers G5 · authority: `fonttools` · fixture: `recursive-vf`</sub>

### `partial.stat-value-exactly-at-new-maximum-is-kept`

**A STAT value sitting exactly on the new maximum survives; one just past it does not**

The boundary is inclusive, because an axis whose maximum is 650 can be rendered at 650. Bold sits at wght 700: with the range 300:700 it is reachable and kept (name ID 409 present, as the previous case shows), and with 300:650 it is not and is dropped. Testing the two sides of the same boundary is what distinguishes a correct inclusive comparison from an off-by-one, and measurement confirms fontTools drops Bold at 300:650 while keeping SemiBold at 600.

<sub>covers G5, G10 · authority: `fonttools` · fixture: `recursive-vf`</sub>

### `partial.stat-values-for-pinned-axis-dropped`

**STAT values on a pinned axis are reduced to the one the pin selects**

The design axis record for MONO stays (see partial.stat-keeps-records-for-pinned-axes) but its two axis values do not both stay: pinning MONO to 0 makes the font a Sans, so 'Sans' at MONO 0 remains true and 'Mono' at MONO 1 becomes unreachable. Keeping both would make the font claim two mutually exclusive styles at once. Measured: name ID 402 'Sans' survives and 403 'Mono' is pruned.

<sub>covers G5, G10 · authority: `fonttools` · fixture: `recursive-vf`</sub>

### `partial.stat-values-outside-restricted-range-dropped`

**STAT axis values beyond the new maximum are dropped**

A STAT axis value names a point on an axis; once the axis no longer reaches that point, the name describes nothing the font can render and a style-matching engine would offer a style that does not exist. Restricting wght to 300:700 must therefore drop ExtraBold, Black and ExtraBlack while keeping Light through Bold. Measured with fontTools: exactly that, and because G10 then prunes the now-unreferenced name records, the dropped values are observable as the absence of name IDs 410, 411 and 412.

<sub>covers G5, G10 · authority: `fonttools` · fixture: `recursive-vf`</sub>

### `partial.surviving-instance-names-retained`

**Name records for instances that survive are retained**

Pruning must be driven by what is still referenced, not by a blanket deletion of high name IDs — the previous case would pass either way. Here eight instances survive, so their subfamily and PostScript name records must survive with them: 338 'Sans Linear Light' and 346 'Sans Linear' stay, while 274 'Mono Linear Light' and 340 'Sans Linear Light Italic' go with their dropped instances. Measured against fontTools, with no dangling IDs left in either direction.

<sub>covers G10, G4 · authority: `fonttools` · fixture: `recursive-vf`</sub>

### `partial.two-axis-fixture-restricted-outlines`

**The minimal two-axis fixture slices to one axis with correct outlines**

Recursive is a real font with avar, feature variations and a five-axis space; when a case on it fails there are several possible causes. The `two-axis` fixture is the same operation with everything else removed, so a failure here isolates the core of partial instancing — rewriting fvar and rescaling gvar — from every other mechanism. It is the case to look at first when the Recursive cases go red.

<sub>covers G2, G13 · authority: `fonttools` · fixture: `two-axis`</sub>

### `partial.variable-kerning-survives-a-restricted-range`

**Variable kerning still interpolates after an axis is narrowed**

A font's variable kerning lives in a `GDEF` item variation store that `GPOS` reaches into by delta-set index. Narrowing an axis without re-tenting that store leaves the regions describing a design space the font no longer has, and the failure is quiet: the kerning is still exactly right at the default location and wrong everywhere else, so text set at any other weight mis-spaces while every outline is perfect. No outline check can see it, and no check that samples a single location can either -- which is why the sampled locations here include an interior one. Measured against fontTools 4.62.1 on this fixture at wght 400, 550 and 700, the pair values are -40/-64/-88 for A/V and -60/-87/-114 for T/A; an implementation that dropped the store would report the 400 column at all three.

<sub>covers G2, G13 · authority: `fonttools` · fixture: `gdef-varstore`</sub>

### `partial.vertical-metrics-still-vary-across-a-restricted-range`

**Ascender, x-height and the underline still move across a narrowed axis**

`MVAR` is what makes the font-wide metrics -- ascender, descender, x-height, cap height, underline -- move with weight or optical size. Narrowing an axis has to re-tent its item variation store, exactly as `HVAR` and `GDEF` do, and bake the residual at the new default into the `OS/2` and `post` fields each record names. This implementation used to apply the table at the new default and then drop it, which left every metric correct at that one location and frozen everywhere else: a font narrowed to wght 300:700 kept its 300 x-height at 700. fontTools keeps the table, so the original passes. Measured on this fixture, x-height runs 526 / 534 / 538 across the three sampled weights and the underline -205 / -188 / -179; an implementation that dropped MVAR would report the first column three times, which is why the samples are not all at the default.

<sub>covers G2, G13 · authority: `fonttools` · fixture: `recursive-vf`</sub>

## static-instancing

Pinning every axis, which is what most people come to Slice for: one weight, frozen, ready to hand to a design application. The output has no axes left, so everything that described variation has to go, and everything that described the font's identity has to be brought up to date.

Covers claims: A1, A3, B3, G1, G10, G11, G12, G13, G3, G5, G6, G7, G8, G9.

### `static.composites.maxp-and-bbox`

**Composite maxp fields and bounding boxes are recalculated through the component tree**

maxCompositePoints, maxCompositeContours, maxComponentElements and maxComponentDepth are defined by the OpenType specification over the flattened component tree, and a composite's own bounding box has to be derived from its components after their offsets have been changed by gvar - a rasteriser that trusts a stale composite bbox will clip. The roster fixture nests one composite two deep, so maxComponentDepth must be 2. Verified in fontTools 4.62.1 on an equivalent purpose-built font: maxp.recalc walked the nesting to depth 2 and the head box picked up the accent lifted by a nested component's offset.

<sub>covers G8 · authority: `spec` · fixture: `composites`</sub>

### `static.composites.outlines-match-source`

**Composite outlines at the pinned location match the source drawn there**

For a composite, gvar deltas move component offsets rather than points, which is a separate code path from simple-glyph interpolation and the one most likely to be got wrong - an off-by-one in the phantom-point count silently shifts an accent. Drawing the instance and the source at the same location and comparing the resulting paths tests the composite after resolution, so it catches both a wrong offset and a wrongly interpolated component. Verified in fontTools 4.62.1: a component offset of 200,0 with a delta of 30,10 came out at 230,10 in the instance, matching the source evaluated at that location.

<sub>covers G13 · authority: `fonttools` · fixture: `composites`</sub>

### `static.composites.survive-as-composites`

**Composite glyphs are not decomposed by static instancing**

Decomposition is a lossless-looking change that is not free: it multiplies the point count, defeats the hinting a composite inherits from its components, and grows the file, so instancing must not do it as a side effect. gvar deltas for a composite apply to component offsets, and applying them requires nothing more than rewriting those offsets, so there is no technical reason to flatten. Verified in fontTools 4.62.1 on a purpose-built composite variable font: at the default overlap mode both a plain and a two-deep nested composite came through the instancer still composite, with their component offsets moved by the deltas (200,0 became 230,10).

<sub>covers G1, G13 · authority: `fonttools` · fixture: `composites`</sub>

### `static.dsig-deleted`

**DSIG is deleted from a static instance**

DSIG is a digital signature over the font's own bytes; instancing rewrites glyf, hmtx, head, maxp, OS/2 and the table directory, so any signature carried over is guaranteed invalid, and the OpenType specification is explicit that the signature covers the whole font file. Shipping an invalid signature is worse than shipping none: Windows treats a broken DSIG as a tampered font. Verified in fontTools 4.62.1, where `instantiateVariableFont` deletes DSIG unconditionally before it touches anything else. The fixture is `with-dsig` rather than `recursive-vf`, which carries no signature and left this case asserting the absence of something that was never there.

<sub>covers G11 · authority: `spec` · fixture: `with-dsig`</sub>

### `static.head.bbox-recalculated-at-default`

**The head bounding box is recalculated at the default location**

The OpenType head specification defines xMin/yMin/xMax/yMax as the union of all glyph bounding boxes; applications use it to size caches and to compute a fallback line box, so a box inherited from the variable font describes the wrong font. recursive-vf's source head box is -275,-330,2380,1125, left over from the unsubsetted family. Verified in fontTools 4.62.1: after pinning every axis at the fvar default the box is 75,-10,565,536, the union of the two non-empty glyphs, recomputed by maxp.recalc during save.

<sub>covers G8 · authority: `spec` · fixture: `recursive-vf`</sub>

### `static.head.bbox-recalculated-at-extreme`

**The head bounding box tracks the instanced outlines at an extreme location**

The bounding box is not a property of the font file but of the instance, and the whole point of recalculating it is that different locations give different answers - at MONO=1 CASL=1 wght=1000 slnt=-15 CRSV=1 the slanted, heaviest outlines reach left of the origin. Asserting a second, different box is what distinguishes genuine recalculation from a lucky constant. Verified in fontTools 4.62.1: the box is -23,-11,596,562 at that location, against 75,-10,565,536 at the default.

<sub>covers G8, G13 · authority: `spec` · fixture: `recursive-vf`</sub>

### `static.head.flags-bit1-recalculated`

**head flags bit 1 is recomputed from the final left side bearings**

head.flags bit 1 asserts that every glyph's left side bearing equals its xMin, and the OpenType specification lets a rasteriser take shortcuts on that promise; instancing moves outlines and rewrites hmtx, so the promise has to be re-tested rather than inherited. Verified in fontTools 4.62.1: maxp.recalc sets the bit when every non-empty glyph has lsb == xMin and clears it otherwise, and for a fully pinned recursive-vf head.flags is 3 - bit 0 (baseline at y=0) from the source plus the recomputed bit 1. The whole field is asserted because the check vocabulary's bit_set covers only fsSelection and macStyle.

<sub>covers G8 · authority: `spec` · fixture: `recursive-vf`</sub>

### `static.hhea.extremes-recalculated-at-default`

**hhea's extremes are recalculated from the instanced hmtx and glyf**

The OpenType hhea specification defines advanceWidthMax, minLeftSideBearing, minRightSideBearing and xMaxExtent as maxima and minima over the font's actual horizontal metrics, and layout engines use xMaxExtent to decide how far a glyph may paint outside its advance. recursive-vf inherits 2400/-275/-289/2380 from the unsubsetted family, which describes glyphs this font does not contain. Verified in fontTools 4.62.1: at the default location the output reads 600/75/35/565, and numberOfHMetrics collapses to 1 because all three advances are 600.

<sub>covers G8 · authority: `spec` · fixture: `recursive-vf`</sub>

### `static.hhea.extremes-recalculated-at-extreme`

**hhea's extremes differ at a different pinned location**

As with the head box, a single location cannot tell a recalculated value from a coincidence. At the heaviest slanted corner of recursive-vf's design space the left side bearing goes negative while the advance stays 600, so three of the four extremes change and one does not - exactly the pattern that catches a partial recalculation. Verified in fontTools 4.62.1: 600/-23/4/596 at MONO=1 CASL=1 wght=1000 slnt=-15 CRSV=1.

<sub>covers G8, G13 · authority: `spec` · fixture: `recursive-vf`</sub>

### `static.hinting.control-tables-preserved`

**fpgm, prep and cvt survive static instancing**

The control-value program, the font program and the control value table are not variation data: they are the font's hinting, and nothing about pinning an axis makes them invalid. Deleting them would silently unhint the instance, which changes rendering at small sizes on every rasteriser that runs the interpreter. Verified in fontTools 4.62.1 on a purpose-built hinted variable font: fpgm, prep and cvt all came through a full pin byte for byte. Where a cvar is present its deltas are folded into cvt and only cvar is removed - a cvt entry of 700 became 730 - which is the same 'apply, then drop' rule as MVAR.

<sub>covers G1, G8 · authority: `fonttools` · fixture: `hinted`</sub>

### `static.hinting.glyph-programs-preserved`

**Per-glyph instructions survive static instancing unchanged**

TrueType instructions address points by index, and instancing changes coordinates but never the number or order of points, so the programs remain meaningful and must be kept. They are not re-generated for the instance either: the hints were authored against the default outlines, and at another location they will be doing approximately, not exactly, the right thing - a known limitation of instancing that the corpus records rather than pretends away. Verified in fontTools 4.62.1: a six-byte glyph program survived instancing and save byte for byte.

<sub>covers G1, G8 · authority: `fonttools` · fixture: `hinted`</sub>

### `static.hinting.maxp-instruction-limits-cover-the-programs`

**maxp's instruction limits still cover the programs the instance carries**

maxp.maxSizeOfInstructions sizes the interpreter's instruction buffer, and the OpenType specification requires it to be at least the largest glyph program in the font. This is the one part of maxp that instancing does not recompute: fontTools' maxp.recalc documents and implements 'recalculate ... most other maxp values except for the TT instructions values', and a deliberately falsified maxSizeOfInstructions of 1 in front of a six-byte program survived a full pin and save unchanged in fontTools 4.62.1. So the claim in G8 that maxp is recalculated is true of the point and contour maxima and false of the instruction maxima; the property that must hold either way is coverage, which is what this case asserts.

<sub>covers G8 · authority: `spec` · fixture: `hinted`</sub>

### `static.italicangle.fractional-slnt`

**A fractional slnt pin is carried into post.italicAngle without rounding**

Unlike usWeightClass, post.italicAngle is a Fixed 16.16 field, so it can hold the fractional coordinate exactly and there is no reason to round it; the caret slope a renderer derives from it would visibly disagree with the outlines if it were rounded to a whole degree. Verified in fontTools 4.62.1: pinning slnt=-7.5 gives italicAngle exactly -7.5, and slnt=-0.5 gives -0.5. The contrast with the wght cases is deliberate - two registered axes, two different numeric contracts, both spelled out.

<sub>covers G7, B3 · authority: `spec` · fixture: `recursive-vf`</sub>

### `static.italicangle.from-slnt-extreme`

**post.italicAngle follows a slnt pin**

The OpenType specification defines the registered slnt axis in counter-clockwise degrees from the vertical, and post.italicAngle in exactly the same units and sign convention, so an oblique instance whose italicAngle is left at 0 lies to every application that uses it - synthetic italic, underline slanting and caret placement all read it. recursive-vf's source post.italicAngle is 0.0, so a pin at the slnt minimum must change it. Verified in fontTools 4.62.1: pinning slnt=-15 gives italicAngle -15.0.

<sub>covers G7 · authority: `spec` · fixture: `recursive-vf`</sub>

### `static.italicangle.upright-stays-zero`

**Pinning slnt at 0 leaves post.italicAngle at zero**

The rule has to be idempotent at the upright end or every non-slanted instance of a slnt-bearing family acquires a spurious angle. slnt=0 is the fvar default here, and the OpenType specification's convention makes 0 degrees the upright value for both slnt and italicAngle, so the correct output is the value the font already had. Verified in fontTools 4.62.1: italicAngle is 0.0 after pinning slnt=0.

<sub>covers G7 · authority: `spec` · fixture: `recursive-vf`</sub>

### `static.load.ttf-accepted`

**A TrueType variable font is accepted and sliced**

A1 makes acceptance of an input exactly the question 'can fontTools.ttLib.TTFont open it', with no format sniffing of the tool's own. This case is the positive half of that contract: a well-formed sfnt with an fvar table must be opened, sliced and written without complaint. It is the floor every other case in this area stands on, so it is worth failing separately rather than as a confusing side effect of some later expectation.

<sub>covers A1, A3, G1 · authority: `slice-ui` · fixture: `recursive-vf`</sub>

### `static.load.woff-input`

**A WOFF input slices to the same static instance as the TTF**

A3 rests on TTFont dispatching on the container, so a WOFF input must be decompressed and instanced exactly as its uncompressed twin: WOFF is a lossless repackaging of the same sfnt tables, and the OpenType/WOFF specification requires the decoded tables to be byte-recoverable. Verified in fontTools 4.62.1: slicing Recursive-VF.subset.woff and Recursive-VF.subset.ttf at the same location produced identical glyph coordinates, hmtx, head bbox, maxp and table set. Any divergence would mean the container, not the design space, changed the outlines.

<sub>covers A1, A3, G1, G13 · authority: `fonttools` · fixture: `recursive-vf-woff`</sub>

### `static.load.woff2-input`

**A WOFF2 input slices to the same static instance as the TTF**

WOFF2 applies a transform to glyf and loca, so unlike WOFF it is not a byte-for-byte repackaging and is the container most likely to perturb outlines; the WOFF2 specification nevertheless requires the transform to reconstruct the original glyph outlines exactly. Verified in fontTools 4.62.1: Recursive-VF.subset.woff2 sliced at MONO=0 CASL=1 wght=700 produced glyph coordinates, hmtx, head bbox and maxp identical to the TTF sliced at the same location. This is the case that would catch a reconstruction bug being mistaken for an instancing bug.

<sub>covers A1, A3, G1, G13 · authority: `fonttools` · fixture: `recursive-vf-woff2`</sub>

### `static.maxp.recalculated-from-final-outlines`

**maxp is recalculated from the instanced outlines, not carried over**

maxp declares the buffers a TrueType rasteriser must allocate before it touches a glyph, so the OpenType specification requires its maxima to describe the glyf table actually present; a stale maxp is a correctness problem, not a size problem, because an under-reported maxPoints leaves the interpreter's point array short. recursive-vf as committed carries maxp values inherited from the unsubsetted family - maxPoints 392, maxContours 22, maxCompositePoints 291, maxComponentElements 4, maxComponentDepth 1 - none of which describe its three glyphs. Verified in fontTools 4.62.1: after a full pin and save, maxp reads 102/2/0/0/0/0, recomputed by maxp.recalc during compile.

<sub>covers G8 · authority: `spec` · fixture: `recursive-vf`</sub>

### `static.mvar.applied-then-deleted`

**MVAR deltas are baked into the metrics tables before MVAR is dropped**

MVAR carries deltas for named metrics in OS/2, post, hhea and vhea; the OpenType specification's whole design is that the static values in those tables are the default-instance values, and an instance at another location must have the deltas applied or it silently ships the default's underline, strikeout and x-height. Dropping the table without applying it is the failure mode this case exists to catch - the table set would look right and the numbers would be wrong. Verified in fontTools 4.62.1: at wght=1000 with the other four axes at default, post.underlinePosition moves from -205 to -145, underlineThickness from 45 to 150, OS/2.sxHeight from 526 to 550, yStrikeoutPosition from 284 to 314 and yStrikeoutSize from 45 to 80, and MVAR is gone.

<sub>covers G1, G8 · authority: `spec` · fixture: `recursive-vf`</sub>

### `static.mvar.default-location-leaves-metrics-alone`

**At the default location MVAR removal changes no metric**

The OpenType specification defines the values stored in OS/2, post and hhea as those of the default instance, so applying MVAR at the default must be a no-op; a case that only ever checks a moved value cannot tell 'applied correctly' from 'applied twice' or 'applied with the wrong sign'. Pairing this with static.mvar.applied-then-deleted brackets the arithmetic from both sides. Verified in fontTools 4.62.1: at the fvar default the five metrics that move at wght=1000 read exactly the source values 526, 284, 45, -205 and 45.

<sub>covers G1, G8 · authority: `spec` · fixture: `recursive-vf`</sub>

### `static.os2.xavgcharwidth-recalculated`

**OS/2.xAvgCharWidth is recalculated for the instance**

For OS/2 version 3 and later the specification defines xAvgCharWidth as the arithmetic mean of the advance widths of all non-zero-width glyphs, so it is a function of hmtx and must be recomputed once instancing has resolved the advances. recursive-vf declares 628, a figure inherited from the full family; its three surviving glyphs all advance 600. Verified in fontTools 4.62.1: instantiateVariableFont calls OS/2.recalcAvgCharWidth and the output reads 600 at every location tested.

<sub>covers G9 · authority: `spec` · fixture: `recursive-vf`</sub>

### `static.outlines.coordinates-finite-and-contours-intact`

**Instanced outlines are finite and keep their contour structure**

glyf coordinates are 16-bit integers, so there is no representation for a non-finite value; a NaN reaching the outline pipeline - from a NaN pin, or from a division by a zero-width delta region - either raises on compile or writes a nonsense integer, and this check names that failure directly rather than letting it surface as a mismatched outline. Contour count is a structural invariant of interpolation: deltas move points, they never add, remove or merge contours, so recursive-vf's 'a' must still have exactly two. Verified in fontTools 4.62.1 at every location tested.

<sub>covers G13, G8 · authority: `spec` · fixture: `recursive-vf`</sub>

### `static.outlines.match-source-at-avar-bent-interior`

**Outlines at an interior location match, with avar and fractional coordinates in play**

Interior locations are the ones avar actually changes: recursive-vf's wght segment map moves normalized 0.2857 to 0.3400, so an implementation that skipped avar would produce outlines that are subtly too light or too heavy, in a way that neither the default nor the extremes would reveal. Pairing that with a fractional slnt coordinate also exercises interpolation between delta regions rather than landing on a master. This is the case that distinguishes 'applies the deltas' from 'applies the deltas at the right coordinate'.

<sub>covers G13, G3 · authority: `fonttools` · fixture: `recursive-vf`</sub>

### `static.outlines.match-source-at-default`

**Outlines at the default location match the source drawn at the default**

This is the identity case for G13: pinning every axis at its fvar default must reproduce the default instance exactly, because the OpenType specification defines glyf as holding the default-instance outlines and all deltas at the default are zero. Any deviation means deltas were applied where none should have been, or the normalization of the default coordinate is not landing on zero. Advances are checked alongside because hmtx and the phantom points are resolved by the same machinery.

<sub>covers G13 · authority: `fonttools` · fixture: `recursive-vf`</sub>

### `static.outlines.match-source-at-extreme`

**Outlines at the far corner of the design space match the source drawn there**

The corner where all five axes are at an extreme is where every delta set contributes at full scale and where the region-scalar products are largest, so a sign error or a mis-ordered axis shows up here at maximum amplitude. It is also the location whose outlines differ most from the stored default, which makes the comparison meaningful rather than nearly trivial. Verified in fontTools 4.62.1 that this location produces materially different outlines - the head box moves from 75,-10,565,536 to -23,-11,596,562.

<sub>covers G13 · authority: `fonttools` · fixture: `recursive-vf`</sub>

### `static.outlines.single-axis-at-maximum`

**The same one-axis font instances at the top of its range**

The companion to the previous case: with the default at the minimum, the maximum is the only location where deltas apply at full scale, so it is the only place the delta arithmetic is exercised at all on this fixture. Pinning there must both interpolate the outlines and rewrite usWeightClass, which for a wght axis the OpenType specification puts on the same scale as the coordinate. Between the two cases the fixture's entire design space is covered.

<sub>covers G7, G13 · authority: `fonttools` · fixture: `single-axis-min-default`</sub>

### `static.outlines.single-axis-default-at-minimum`

**An axis whose default equals its minimum instances correctly at that default**

When the default sits at the axis minimum the negative half of the normalized range is empty, so every delta region has a zero-width lower side; an implementation that divides by the region width without guarding it produces a division by zero or a NaN exactly here. This is the shape Recursive's own wght axis has, which makes it worth isolating in a one-axis fixture where nothing else can mask it. The correct answer is the plain one: pinning at the default reproduces the stored default outlines and leaves a static font.

<sub>covers G1, G13 · authority: `fonttools` · fixture: `single-axis-min-default`</sub>

### `static.overlap.composites-flagged`

**OVERLAP_COMPOUND is set on composites of a static instance**

A composite whose components overlap - the accent of a precomposed letter crossing its base is the everyday case - needs the same non-zero fill promise, and the OpenType glyf specification puts it in a different flag, OVERLAP_COMPOUND (0x400), carried on a component rather than a point. Verified in fontTools 4.62.1 (setMacOverlapFlags): the flag is set on the first component only, not on every component, for both the plain and the two-deep nested composite in a purpose-built test font. A checker that demanded it on all components would wrongly fail conformant output.

<sub>covers G12 · authority: `fonttools` · fixture: `composites`</sub>

### `static.overlap.simple-glyphs-flagged`

**OVERLAP_SIMPLE is set on every simple glyph of a static instance**

Variable fonts are normally drawn with overlapping contours, and the OpenType glyf specification's OVERLAP_SIMPLE flag on the first point tells a rasteriser to fill with the non-zero rule; Apple's rasterisers honour it and, without it, an interpolated instance can render with holes where strokes cross. Setting it unconditionally is what fontTools does at the default overlap mode and what the original therefore inherits, and it is safe because a non-overlapping outline fills identically under either rule. Verified in fontTools 4.62.1: after a full pin, both contoured glyphs of recursive-vf have flag 0x40 on point 0, while the empty .notdef gets nothing because it has no points.

<sub>covers G12 · authority: `fonttools` · fixture: `recursive-vf`</sub>

### `static.pin-all.dead-feature-variation-dropped`

**A feature variation that cannot hold at the pinned location leaves no lookups behind**

The mirror of the previous case: at the fvar default nothing in recursive-vf's rvrn condition set is satisfied, so the italic substitution must not fire in the instance. If the lookups were folded in unconditionally the upright instance would shape 'a' as 'a.italic' - a visible, silent corruption. Verified in fontTools 4.62.1: at the default location the output GSUB has no FeatureVariations, an empty LookupList, and no rvrn feature record at all.

<sub>covers G1, G6 · authority: `fonttools` · fixture: `recursive-vf`</sub>

### `static.pin-all.drops-avar`

**Pinning every axis removes avar**

avar exists only to remap the normalized value of an fvar axis, and the OpenType specification requires its axis segment maps to correspond one-to-one, in order, with the fvar axes. A static font has no fvar axes, so an avar would have to be either empty or dangling; either is malformed. Verified in fontTools 4.62.1: avar is absent from the output of a full pin of recursive-vf, whose source avar carries a non-trivial eight-point map on wght and a steep segment on slnt.

<sub>covers G1, G3 · authority: `spec` · fixture: `recursive-vf`</sub>

### `static.pin-all.drops-fvar-and-gvar`

**Pinning every axis removes fvar and gvar**

The OpenType specification defines fvar as the table that declares a font's variation axes and gvar as the table of glyph deltas indexed by them; an fvar with zero axes is not a legal record, and gvar deltas with nothing to interpolate against are unreachable data. Once every axis has a fixed coordinate the deltas have been consumed into the outlines, so keeping them would both bloat the file and let a renderer apply them twice. Verified in fontTools 4.62.1: both tables are absent after instantiateVariableFont with all five Recursive axes pinned.

<sub>covers G1 · authority: `spec` · fixture: `recursive-vf`</sub>

### `static.pin-all.drops-metrics-variation-stores`

**Pinning every axis removes HVAR, VVAR and MVAR**

HVAR, VVAR and MVAR are all item variation stores whose delta-set indices are resolved against a normalized coordinate vector; with no fvar there is no coordinate vector, so per the OpenType specification those tables cannot be interpreted and must not be present. Their content is not discarded but baked in first - see static.mvar.applied-then-deleted - so removing them loses nothing. Verified in fontTools 4.62.1: the output table set after a full pin of recursive-vf contains none of the three. The VVAR expectation is inert for this fixture, which has no vertical metrics, and is stated so that a fixture that gains them is covered.

<sub>covers G1 · authority: `spec` · fixture: `recursive-vf`</sub>

### `static.pin-all.feature-variation-folded-in`

**A feature variation that holds at the pinned location becomes an ordinary feature**

FeatureVariations condition sets are expressed in normalized axis coordinates and are indexed by fvar axis order, so the OpenType specification gives them no meaning in a font without fvar; leaving one behind in a static instance is malformed. A condition that is satisfied at the pinned location is not simply discarded, though - its substitutions are what the user asked for and must survive as a plain feature. Verified in fontTools 4.62.1: pinning recursive-vf at slnt=-15, CRSV=1 leaves GSUB with no FeatureVariations, one lookup, and rvrn mapping a to a.italic.

<sub>covers G1, G6 · authority: `spec` · fixture: `recursive-vf`</sub>

### `static.pin-all.keeps-glyph-set`

**Instancing does not subset the glyph set, the layout tables or the hinting tables**

Instancing narrows the design space, not the character set, and it is a different operation from subsetting; it must not quietly do both, nor drop tables it merely fails to recognise. This matters concretely for recursive-vf, where a.italic is reachable only through a feature-variation substitution: at the default location nothing substitutes it any more, yet dropping the glyph would change what a shaper can produce through other means and would renumber every glyph ID. The gasp and prep expectations guard the same property from the other side - a table-allowlist implementation that kept only the tables the corpus names elsewhere would silently unhint the output. Verified in fontTools 4.62.1: numGlyphs stays 3 and cmap, GDEF, GPOS, GSUB, gasp and prep are all still present after a full pin.

<sub>covers G1 · authority: `fonttools` · fixture: `recursive-vf`</sub>

### `static.pin-all.keeps-stat`

**STAT survives a full pin**

STAT is the one variation-related table that is not about interpolation: the OpenType specification requires it in all variable fonts and recommends it in every static font that is part of a variable family, because it is what tells the shell where this instance sits in the family's style space. Removing it alongside fvar would turn a well-described instance into an orphan. Verified in fontTools 4.62.1: after a full pin the STAT table is present, its DesignAxisRecord still lists all five Recursive axes, and only the axis values that do not hold at the pinned location have been dropped.

<sub>covers G1, G5 · authority: `spec` · fixture: `recursive-vf`</sub>

### `static.pin-all.no-dangling-name-ids`

**Axis and instance name records left behind are exactly the ones STAT still uses**

The OpenType name specification reserves IDs 256 and above for font-specific uses referenced from other tables; once fvar is gone, an ID that nothing points at is dead weight that no shell can ever display. The interesting part is that a full pin does not strip all of them: STAT keeps its design axis records, so the five axis nameIDs stay referenced and must survive. Verified in fontTools 4.62.1: a fully pinned recursive-vf retains nameIDs 269-273 (the axis names, referenced by STAT DesignAxisRecord) plus the surviving STAT axis-value names, and drops the sixty-four instance subfamily names that fvar used to own.

<sub>covers G1, G5, G10 · authority: `spec` · fixture: `recursive-vf`</sub>

### `static.usweightclass.centred-default-extreme`

**usWeightClass follows the pin on an axis whose default is centred**

centred-default has wght 100/400/900, so a pin at the maximum is two-thirds of the way up a design space whose two halves normalize at different rates; the weight class is nevertheless read straight off the user-space coordinate and owes nothing to normalization. This is the shape of axis on which an implementation that computed the weight class from the normalized value would be caught out, because 900 normalizes to 1.0 while 250 and 650 both normalize to half. The OpenType specification defines usWeightClass on the same scale as the wght coordinate itself.

<sub>covers G7, G1 · authority: `spec` · fixture: `centred-default`</sub>

### `static.usweightclass.centred-default-minimum`

**usWeightClass follows a pin below the centred default**

The lower half of centred-default's wght axis spans 100 to 400 while the upper spans 400 to 900, so the two sides normalize at different rates and a value below the default is the case an implementation is most likely to mishandle. As above, the OpenType specification puts usWeightClass on the wght axis's own scale, so the answer is simply the pinned number. Keeping both halves as separate cases means a sign or direction error shows up as one failure rather than none.

<sub>covers G7, G1 · authority: `spec` · fixture: `centred-default`</sub>

### `static.usweightclass.from-pin-interior`

**usWeightClass follows a wght pin between the axis extremes**

The same rule at an interior coordinate, which is where it actually bites: recursive-vf's wght axis has its default at the minimum (300), so every instance except the lightest needs usWeightClass rewritten. A Regular sliced out of this family must declare 400, or every OS style-matcher will file it as Light. Verified in fontTools 4.62.1: usWeightClass is 400 after pinning wght=400.

<sub>covers G7 · authority: `spec` · fixture: `recursive-vf`</sub>

### `static.usweightclass.from-pin-max`

**usWeightClass follows a wght pin at the axis maximum**

The OpenType specification says the registered wght axis and OS/2.usWeightClass express the same quantity on the same 1-1000 scale, and that an instance's usWeightClass should match its wght coordinate; a font left declaring the variable font's default weight would sort and substitute as the wrong weight everywhere. recursive-vf's source usWeightClass is 300, so a pin at 1000 must change it. Verified in fontTools 4.62.1 (varLib.set_default_weight_width_slant): the output reads 1000.

<sub>covers G7 · authority: `spec` · fixture: `recursive-vf`</sub>

### `static.usweightclass.is-userspace-not-avar-mapped`

**usWeightClass is the coordinate the user typed, not the avar-mapped one**

avar remaps normalized coordinates to redistribute interpolation; it says nothing about what the design-space label means. The OpenType specification defines usWeightClass in user-space weight units, so it must be read off the pin before normalization - recursive-vf's avar bends wght hard (normalized 0.4286 maps to 0.4286 but 0.2857 maps to 0.3400), and taking the mapped value would produce a weight class that no user asked for. Verified in fontTools 4.62.1: pinning wght=600, a coordinate that avar demonstrably moves, still yields usWeightClass 600.

<sub>covers G7, G3 · authority: `spec` · fixture: `recursive-vf`</sub>

### `static.usweightclass.rounds-fractional-pin`

**A fractional wght pin rounds to an integer usWeightClass**

fvar axis coordinates are Fixed 16.16 and can legitimately be fractional, but OS/2.usWeightClass is a uint16, so some rounding rule must be applied and it must be stated rather than left to whatever the language's float-to-int does. fontTools uses otRound, which is round-half-up: 350.5 goes to 351, where Python's own round() and any round-half-to-even implementation would give 350. That difference is why the value probed here is a half-way one - it is the only kind of input on which the two conventions disagree. Verified in fontTools 4.62.1.

<sub>covers G7, B3 · authority: `fonttools` · fixture: `recursive-vf`</sub>

### `static.uswidthclass.between-nodes-rounds-up`

**wdth=70 gives usWidthClass 3, not 2**

70 lies between the Extra-condensed node at 62.5 and the Condensed node at 75, so the piecewise-linear map gives 2.6, which rounds to 3; an implementation that floored, or that treated the map as a lookup of the nearest lower node, would answer 2. The OpenType specification names only the nine anchors and says nothing about values between them, so this is fontTools' documented rule rather than a spec requirement, and it is what the original inherits. Verified in fontTools 4.62.1. Requires two-axis's wdth axis to include 70.

<sub>covers G7 · authority: `fonttools` · fixture: `two-axis`</sub>

### `static.uswidthclass.normal`

**wdth=100 gives usWidthClass 5**

The OpenType specification tabulates usWidthClass 1-9 against nine named widths from Ultra-condensed to Ultra-expanded, and pairs class 5 (Medium/normal) with a wdth of 100%; the registered wdth axis is defined as a percentage of normal width, so 100 must map to 5. Verified in fontTools 4.62.1 against WDTH_VALUE_TO_OS2_WIDTH_CLASS. This case and the five that follow require the two-axis fixture's wdth axis to span the full registered 50-200 range with default 100, because fontTools clamps a pin to the axis extent before mapping and a narrower fixture would silently test a different value.

<sub>covers G7 · authority: `spec` · fixture: `two-axis`</sub>

### `static.uswidthclass.ultra-condensed`

**wdth=50 gives usWidthClass 1**

50% is the OpenType specification's Ultra-condensed anchor and the bottom of the registered wdth range, so it maps to class 1; it is also the endpoint that a clamping bug would move, since fontTools clamps the value into 50..200 before mapping. Verified in fontTools 4.62.1: piecewiseLinearMap over the nine registered nodes gives 1 at 50, and any pin below 50 clamps to 1 as well. Requires two-axis's wdth axis to reach 50.

<sub>covers G7 · authority: `spec` · fixture: `two-axis`</sub>

### `static.uswidthclass.untouched-without-wdth-axis`

**A font with no wdth axis keeps the usWidthClass it had**

The rewrite is keyed on the axis being present in the pinned location, not on the field existing: recursive-vf has MONO, CASL, wght, slnt and CRSV but no wdth, so there is no width information to derive and the font's own declaration must stand. An implementation that reset usWidthClass to a default of 5 whenever it wrote an instance would be wrong for any condensed family, and would be invisible here only by coincidence. Verified in fontTools 4.62.1: usWidthClass is 5 before and after, because set_default_weight_width_slant never enters the wdth branch.

<sub>covers G7 · authority: `fonttools` · fixture: `recursive-vf`</sub>

### `static.uswidthclass.upper-segment-is-not-linear`

**wdth=120 gives usWidthClass 7, showing the map is piecewise and not linear in wdth**

A naive linear map from 50..200 onto 1..9 would put 120 at about 4.7; the real map is piecewise over nine unevenly spaced nodes, and between 112.5 (class 6) and 125 (class 7) the value 120 gives 6.6, which rounds to 7. This is the single best case for catching an implementation that reimplemented the mapping as arithmetic instead of a table. Verified in fontTools 4.62.1. Requires two-axis's wdth axis to include 120.

<sub>covers G7 · authority: `fonttools` · fixture: `two-axis`</sub>

### `static.uswidthclass.wide-segment-half-way`

**wdth=175 gives usWidthClass 9**

The last two nodes are 150 (class 8) and 200 (class 9), fifty units apart where the lower segments are 12.5 apart, so 175 sits exactly half way and the map yields 8.5; otRound is round-half-up, so the answer is 9 rather than the 8 that round-half-to-even would give. This is the only half-way point in the whole map, which makes it the case that pins down the rounding rule for widths. Verified in fontTools 4.62.1. Requires two-axis's wdth axis to reach 175.

<sub>covers G7 · authority: `fonttools` · fixture: `two-axis`</sub>

## Coverage

The behaviour map declares 61 claims. 10 of them describe the running application rather than the font it produces and cannot be reached by a headless corpus; of the 51 that remain, **51 have at least one case**.

Claims out of scope for this corpus, and what each one is:

- **A4** — the status bar text after a successful load
- **F4** — the warning when the path field no longer matches the loaded font
- **F5** — the "Canceled" status after dismissing the save dialog
- **F6** — that the work runs on a QThreadPool behind a modal progress indicator
- **I1** — the File menu and its Ctrl+O accelerator
- **I2** — the References menu's specification links
- **I3** — the Help menu
- **I4** — drag and drop onto the font-path field
- **I5** — the version number in the status bar
- **I6** — the window dropping its title and logo on a short screen

Testing these means driving the Qt application through a display, which is a
different harness from this one. They are recorded in the behaviour map so
that a reimplementation knows they exist, not because the corpus checks them.
